The Buddha requested two branches as a loan, vowing to establish the conditions for their future use. At that time, as the Buddha entered the city, Sudhana took the flowers and offered them to the Buddha, scattering them upon the Buddha’s crown.
By the power of his vow, they formed into a parasol that followed the Buddha wherever he went or stayed.
Through the Buddha’s supernormal power, the ground appeared to be covered in mud; Sudhana spread his hair over it, making this aspiration: "May the Buddha tread upon my body."
He granted me the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood. Having not received such a prediction, I would never have risen from this place.
Then Dīpaṃkara arrived and stepped over my body; he forbade the crowd from treading upon it and then bestowed the prophecy, saying: "This māṇava, in a future age..."
"You shall attain Buddhahood, named Śākyamuni, endowed with the ten titles, no different from me.

After the Buddha had bestowed this prediction, [the practitioner] immediately ascended to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Now tell me: what was the World-Honored One pointing to by bringing forth these worn-out vines?

First, it was to provide a seal of certification for the occasion, causing sentient beings to have faith; second, it was to demonstrate that there is nothing to be attained, thereby clarifying the truth.
The principle of non-abiding may be said to be like a single drop of ink that forms two dragons. Question:
Previously, in the chapter on the detachment from marks regarding the fruit-dharmas, it was asked: "Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Since this has already been asked, why is it asked again here? Answer:
The preceding question—"Even dharma should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharma"—is explained as clarifying the principle that the Perfection of Wisdom transcends all marks;
it asks whether that which is attained at the stage of Buddhahood is existent or non-existent.

This question is explained as showing that what is called "Buddha-dharma" is not, in fact, Buddha-dharma, thereby clarifying the meaning of the mind abiding in non-abiding. This is then addressed from the perspective of the causal stage of a Buddha...
Regarding the question of whether one has attained or not attained the Dharma: the previous question concerned the self-realized Bodhi within the Buddha-fruit;
this present question concerns the Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit sought through practice during the causal stage of a Tathāgata. Since their meanings are distinct, they are not redundant.
△ Third, the Adornments of the Bodhisattva.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely designated as 'adorning.'"
This concludes the section on the Bodhisattva’s realization of the distinctions within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

From the passage beginning with "Subhūti," it means that since you already know that within the unconditioned dharmas, the Buddha truly attained nothing from Dīpaṃkara, it can be understood that when the Buddha was a bodhisattva...
"Is it not through three great *asaṃkhyeya*-kalpas and the practice of the six *pāramitās* that the adornment of Buddha-fields occurs? "No, World-Honored One.
[The Master] says this because, within the realm of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, there is in reality no such thing as the adornment of Buddha-fields.
"Why is this? he asks, explaining the reason for his "no. He states that what is called "adornment" refers to purifying one's own mind; [this is the true] Buddha-field.
This refers to the Land of Purity of Mind. Subhūti has already understood that purity is the mind; since the Buddha-land is pure only when the mind is pure, he answered "no.
As for "adorned Buddha-lands," this is spoken according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) regarding the land of true retribution (vipāka-bhūmi).
Because it is adorned by the merit and wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices, it is not non-existent; therefore, it is so described.
"There is adornment, yet it is not adornment. This clarifies the Dharma-nature land from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

It is the ground of pure nature (*viśuddha-bhūmi*), the true realm of tranquil light (*jig-kō*). It is one's own mind. As for its essence, it transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and is beyond the hundred negations;
it cannot be known by intellect, nor can it be expressed in words. This precisely refers to the cessation of mental activity (*citta-gati*).
The path is cut off; words and the Way are severed. Since even the formless cannot be discussed or measured, how could one speak of the adornment of forms?
If it were so, it would be like driving a wedge into empty space or painting eyebrows on a primordial chaos. Thus, one knows that the source of the mind is not characterized by form;
how then could earth be adorned? Therefore, it is said: "It is precisely not adornment; it is called adornment."

This refers to the simultaneous integration of the two truths. Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), true emptiness does not obstruct wondrous existence, and wondrous existence does not obstruct true emptiness.
Although one abides within the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), fundamentally there is no "adornment" to be obtained.
If, at present, the gateway is brilliantly adorned, even though there is no reality to the adornment, yet the designation "adornment" is not discarded;

therefore it is said, "This is called adornment. One must know that "it is not adornment" means not grasping at dharmas, which is the absence of the mark of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). "This is called adornment" means not grasping at non-dharmas. This is...
Nor is there any characteristic of non-dharma. △ Second, the explicit clarification of non-abiding:
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this manner. They should not give rise to a mind by abiding in form;
they should not give rise to a mind by abiding in sound, odor, taste, touch, or dharmas. They should give rise [to a mind] without abiding anywhere.
Regarding the phrase "its mind":

these two characters serve as the concluding terms for the fixed definition. This is because, from the preceding brief indications and extensive explanations, beginning with the holy fruits of the Hīnayāna up to the dharmas attained by the Buddha, the various adornments of the Bodhisattva have been analyzed in detail. There is nothing [further to be said].
Not all [commentators] have clarified the meaning of non-abiding. Reaching this point, he concludes by saying:
"Therefore, Subhūti, when you first asked me how one should abide, I replied that one should abide in this way. Furthermore, he briefly indicates it as follows:
"A Bodhisattva should not dwell on any phenomenon; indeed, a Bodhisattva should simply dwell as instructed.
These words of the initial question and answer by Subhūti constitute the formal conclusion. Therefore, it says:
"All Bodhisattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this manner. The term "in this manner" refers back to what has been briefly shown and extensively explained above.
This refers to the various passages concerning non-abiding. As for "giving rise to purity," it means being clear without turbidity and pure without defilement.
If even a single thought of attachment arises within the Bodhisattva’s mind, it immediately becomes turbid and defiled, and cannot be called pure.
If this is so, how does one give rise to a pure mind? Simply by not being stained by [any single thing] throughout the twelve periods of the day and night.
Dust does not defile a single dharma; it is pure and abundant, naked and clear. This is precisely the mind that arises without dwelling upon form and the other sense objects.
With this wondrous mind of prajñā, one is like a pure, bright mirror. If one dwells upon even a single speck of dust, one's luminosity will be defiled by that speck of dust.
If one does not dwell upon even a single speck of dust, then all things are reflected therein. This is truly what is meant by "only having..."

"A little bit. This means there is indeed a "little bit. Even if one is naked as a child with not a thread of cloth upon them, and ten thousand miles of sky are cloudless—even such emptiness must receive a blow of the staff;
this is precisely what that refers to. "Responding without dwelling anywhere" is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"Yet giving rise to the mind" is wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*). As for the character "respond" (*ying*), it reverses the above "not responding"; it refers to practicing *dāna* (generosity).
Regarding this, one should not dwell upon these six sense objects at all, nor have any attachment to them.
That which arises [in such a state] is precisely what is called the pure, non-dwelling mind. Practicing *dāna* (generosity) with this, the *Zhengqixin lun* (*Awakening of Faith*) states:

"Because one knows that the essence of the Dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the *pāramitā* of *dāna* in accordance with it. If one gives rise to [this practice] through non-dwelling...

When the mind is considered as a whole, the ultimate and conventional truths merge into one; this is the Middle Way, the First Noble Truth. This is the teaching for bodhisattvas who abide in the mind:
the mind has no place of abiding, yet even "abiding" is not abiding. Birth is non-birth, and non-birth is birth.
Yet, if one engages with even a single thought-moment, the mind becomes attached and the sensory objects enter; this is no longer called "non-abiding," and it leads to...
To have a dwelling place is not called a pure mind; it becomes a defiled mind.
Even if one has the notion of a non-dwelling object, one has already dwelt there. To wish not to dwell on objects, one must not dwell on the mind.

If the mind can truly have no place of dwelling, only then will one know that objects likewise have no location. This is precisely reaching the point where the path ends at the water’s edge and the mountains’ end.
When activity arises, it naturally subsides; when fire reaches its end, the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished, and the remaining embers cool of their own accord.
It is truly thus: though one is born all day long, there is no birth; though one abides all day long, there is no abiding. This non-arising arising does not hinder spontaneous arising;
this non-abiding abiding—what obstacle could there be to abiding in accordance with conditions? Inferring from this, then:
Dressing and eating are nothing other than the scenery of one's own native ground; sending off guests and welcoming visitors fully reveals the countenance of the person themselves.
As it is said, "Every dust mote is a treasure; wherever you go, you encounter Him. Thus, what dharma does not belong to the non-abiding true mind?
What object does not manifest the wondrous essence of Prajñā? Therefore, when the practitioner came forward at the time of begging for food, [he encountered this reality].
When one happens to encounter the Tathāgata’s walking, standing, sitting, or reclining; his movement, stillness, coming, or going;

or even when slightly touching the corner of his *kāṣāya* robe or the vicinity of his alms bowl, and for this reason exclaims that the Buddha is "rare and marvelous," it is precisely within this principle of non-going that one glimpses a fragmentary glimpse.
As for Huangmei attaining the essential meaning and Caoxi’s realization—when compared [to this]...
The capacity of the recipient is the next [factor]. △ Third, the illustration clarifying non-abiding:
"Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be large?
Subhūti said, "It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha says it is 'not a body'; it is merely named 'large'."

Body. This serves as a metaphor for the dharma of bondage. For indeed, the pure mind described in the preceding text is that which all Buddhas have realized, that which Bodhisattvas cultivate, and that which sentient beings are deluded about; it is thus the [boundary] between the ordinary and the sage.
The demarcation of boundaries is the general path for both sentient beings and Buddhas. Thus, to be deluded regarding it leads to the saṃsāra of the six realms;

to awaken to it reveals the secret treasury of the three virtues. Even now, at the assembly in Jeta Grove, the World-Honored One has no separate dharma to preach, but merely points directly to what is inherently possessed by people.
This is why he previously donned his robes, held his bowl, and came and went.
Whether walking or sitting, there is nothing that does not reveal the radiant light of one's original ground.

Although those present at the time may have caught a glimpse of this news, alas, the eyes of the great assembly were dull and their heads were lost in confusion. They merely knew that when it was time to put on robes, they would put on robes along with the crowd;
when it was time to hold the alms bowl, they would hold the bowl along with the crowd. All day long they were busily preoccupied, rising and falling in tandem with others, chasing after them.
Traveling in groups to and fro between Śrāvastī and entering and leaving Jetavana, they did not know where their own original life-source (mūla-cihna) was located.

Therefore, the Venerable One, rejoicing that he himself had realized this while grieving for others who had not yet awakened, with the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in devout sincerity, prostrated with the five limbs touching the ground, joined his palms with a single-minded focus, and suddenly raised three questions—namely, "O son of good family... and so forth.
“O Woman, how should one resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? How should one abide?
How should one subdue [the mind]? Our World-Honored One, being pleased by her question and moved by the sincerity of her request, immediately praised her and granted her wish, saying:
‘Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is just as you have said, even unto you...’”

Listen now attentively; I shall explain for you the principle by which a son or daughter of good family resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, as well as the principles of abiding in such a manner and subduing [the mind] in such a manner.
When the disciple reached this point, he prostrated himself fully and said, "Yes, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, taking the error as the opportunity, answered each of his questions in turn.
Thus, he first responded to the request to dwell in the stages of descent, and next answered the inquiry regarding Bodhi; then, within that initial response, he further expanded upon it.
The two sections have been summarized. First, they were briefly indicated; next, they were further explained in detail and thoroughly elucidated.

The principles of subduing the mind to transcend its marks and dwelling the mind in non-abiding have thus been concluded. Nevertheless, although people employ this non-abiding, pure, true mind in their daily lives, they remain deluded and unaware of it.
Therefore, the World-Honored One skillfully posed a question, employing analogies to illustrate the Dharma.

By borrowing events to manifest principles, it is made easy for sentient beings to know and easy for them to understand. Thus, two interpretations are provided: first, a detailed explanation of the event according to the metaphor;
second, an application of the metaphor to reveal the principle. At the beginning of the sutra, Subhūti says: "Suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains.
Would that body be large? This is not a metaphor used as a metaphor; rather, it is an established illustration.

Suppose there were a person whose body, as a result of their primary retribution (*vipāka*), was as large as Sumeru, the King of Mountains—Sumeru being the Sanskrit term, which in this [Chinese] language means "Wondrous High Mountain.
It is composed of four precious substances, and is thus called "wondrous" (*miao*); it rises alone above all other peaks, and is therefore called "high" (*gao*).
Its base rests upon the diamond-limit (*vajra-maṇḍala*), situated in the center of the four oceans, rising eighty-four thousand [yojanas] above the water.
It is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep within the waters. It is encircled by seven golden mountains and presides over sixty thousand subsidiary mountains as its retinue.
Even though the ocean waves may reach a depth of a thousand fathoms, this mountain remains majestic and unmoving;
therefore, it is named the King of Mountains. What do you think? [The Buddha] poses this question to you, Subhūti: "What is your thought?"
"Would the body of such a person be considered large? The Venerable One replied, "If the size of that body were like Mount Sumeru, it could indeed be called very large, World-Honored One.
This answer was given by the Venerable One as he discussed the matter based on its actual nature.

Because the Tathāgata asked about "greatness," the answer was given in terms of "greatness. Yet the one present according to his capacity (*kālacitta*) knew that the Buddha’s intention did not originally lie therein;
thus, he followed the path back home and uttered a turning phrase, saying: "Though the body may be equal to Mount Sumeru..."
This is still not yet "great. Why is this? The Buddha taught that what is not a body is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*).
This designation of "not a body" as "great" refers to the *dharmakāya*. This *dharmakāya* encompasses all phenomena and includes the entire cosmos;
it is neither large nor small, neither form nor color. Therefore, it is called "not a body," which is precisely what is named the "Great Body. Indeed, the *dharma*...
As for that which is called the "body," in its greatness it is without exterior; in its minuteness it is without interior. It cannot be grasped by form or appearance;
it cannot be seen as a phenomenon of color or matter. It cannot be fathomed by the mind or intellect, nor can it be known through calculation or measurement.

When released, it pervades the six directions; when withdrawn, it retreats and hides within the profound mystery. Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). It does not...
It falls within all numerical categories. This is precisely because it is not a body; being untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called the pure great body.
The above has been a detailed explanation of the matter by means of analogy. If one wishes to apply this to the Dharma to reveal its underlying principle:

Mount Sumeru is composed of four jewels, situated amidst the four seas, encircled by seven golden mountains, and presiding over sixty thousand [minor peaks]. Although there are thousands of waves and ten thousand ripples, [it remains unmoved].

That which cannot be moved is used as a metaphor for this pure mind, which possesses the four virtues of permanence, bliss, selfhood, and quiescence, just as a mountain is composed of the four treasures.
As for the phrase "dwelling in the midst of the four seas," it refers to this mind from time immemorial.
Deluded regarding the truth and pursuing the false, one constantly dwells within the four modes of birth amidst the ocean of afflictions.
That which "encircles the seven mountains of gold and governs the sixty thousand [rivers]" precisely clarifies this mind, which mingles birth-and-death within the seven realms and six paths.
That it "remains unmoved despite the waves" precisely reveals that although this mind exists within the ocean of birth-and-death and afflictions, and amidst the six paths and seven realms...
Within, it has never moved even a hair’s breadth from its original state. As it is said: "It may be rubbed without being worn thin; it may be dyed black without being stained.

It has never been born when arising, nor has it ever ceased when extinguished. Thus, it remains unstained even while within the cycle of birth and death, and yet it is not impure even while abiding in nirvana.
This very "impurity" is precisely the primordial absence of defilement, which cannot be described as pure.
The purity within impurity is true purity; this is precisely the non-abiding, pure, true mind.
As for its essence, it encompasses all phenomena and subsumes the ten realms. Vertically, it penetrates the vastness of suchness; horizontally, it exhausts the limits of the dharma-realm.
When spoken of as small, none in the world can break it; when spoken of as large, none in the world can contain it. Therefore, it is said:
"Very great. Nevertheless, there is still something to be said regarding these two characters, "very great.
For the World-Honored One merely asked whether it was "great," and had the disciple answered simply "great," the matter would have been concluded. Why, then, did he answer "very great"?
One must understand that this single character "very" (*shen*) is the Venerable’s turn of phrase. Its meaning is that although Mount Sumeru is indeed great, it still belongs to...

It is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Among the five categories of phenomena (*dharma*), it is subsumed under form (*rūpa*); within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it is included in the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.
It can be analyzed into spatial parts and reduced to ashes by the fires at the end of an eon (*kalpa*).

Furthermore, the World-Honored One previously taught that "whatever has marks is all false and illusory. Thus, if even the worlds of the ten directions are as such and yet empty, why [speak of] a single mustard seed?
Mount Sumeru recognizes itself as great; thus one knows that the greatness of Mount Sumeru is not yet true greatness. The vastness of the ten directions is not yet true vastness.
That which can encompass the vastness of the ten directions and swallow up the greatness of Mount Sumeru—that alone is true greatness.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddha says that which is not a body is called the Great Body. These two phrases correspond to the preceding: "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere.
If one knows non-dwelling, one immediately recognizes the non-body; if one simply understands the pure mind, one naturally comprehends the Great Body.
This uses the non-body and the Great Body as metaphors for dwelling in non-dwelling. The meaning is that if one dwells in...

Regarding these characteristics: though Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, may be small, it is vast if it has no fixed location; though a single hair-tip may be large, it is minute when compared to this.

At this point, both the dharma and the analogy become manifest, and both principle and phenomenon are fully present. If one explains this by correlating it with the three virtues, then it refers to the pure mind.
The Dharma-body is the virtue of wisdom; "should abide nowhere" is the virtue of prajñā; "purifying the mind while practicing dāna" is the virtue of liberation.
If one were to interpret this by correlating it with the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, then the pure mind is the prajñā of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*);

"should abide nowhere" is the prajñā of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*); and purifying the mind while practicing dāna is the prajñā of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*). Thus, these are three [aspects].
It is not three; it is one, yet not one. It does not obstruct the three paths according to the three [vehicles], nor does it preclude speaking of one from the perspective of the one.
Reaching this point, there is the principle of non-abiding, and no further aggregates remain. What follows below is nothing more than an exhortation to uphold [the teaching] through comparison.
△ Four: Comparing and Revealing Superiority, in two parts. One: Comparison.
"Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied, "They would be very numerous, World-Honored One.
Those Ganges Rivers alone would already be beyond counting, let alone their sands. Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth: if...

"If there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and used them for giving, would they gain much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much, World-Honored One."
Through these various detailed explanations, the principle of non-abiding has now been clearly elucidated.
Therefore, the Tathāgata cites this comparison to manifest the merit of upholding and expounding [this teaching]. However, previously there was only the gift of the jewels of a great trichiliocosm.

Now, as for the gift of the Ganges and a great trichiliocosm of jewels, it is simply because the quantity of the gift is so vast that it further highlights the superior merit of upholding [the teaching] without abiding; there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority between them.
This "Ganges" is also called Gaṅgā, which is translated here as "Coming from Heaven," due to the high elevation of its source. Furthermore, it is said:
The River of Blessings (*Puṇyanadī*): because sentient beings who enter it can generate merit.
To the north of this Jambudvīpa, there are nine Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇagiri*), followed by the Great Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*). Beyond that is Mount Gandhamādana.

To the south of this Mount Gandhamādana and to the north of the Snow-Capped Mountain lies a lake named Anavatapta, which translates as "Free from Heat and Torment. It is fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth.
Ten yojanas [in length]. It is filled with water possessing the eight virtues. The pond has four openings, each one yojana [wide].

From these four openings flow four rivers, each encircling the pond once. They consist of the four kinds of precious colors, unmixed with one another, and flow turbulently into the ocean, each dividing into twenty-five thousand channels.
These great rivers irrigate the four continents. From the eastern "Ox-mouth" opening flows the Gaṅgā...
The Gaṅgā River flows with silver sands intermingled, entering the southeastern sea through the Elephant’s Mouth;

it emerges as the Sindhu River, flowing with golden sands intermingled, entering the southwestern sea through the Horse’s Mouth; it emerges as the Vakṣu River, flowing with lapis lazuli sands intermingled, entering the northwestern sea through the Lion’s Mouth;
and it emerges as the Sītā River, flowing with crystal sands intermingled, entering the northeastern sea.
The Ocean. Here, the word Gaṅgā refers to the river that flows from the Ox’s Mouth; it meanders for forty *li*, and its sand is as fine as flour.
The Buddha once resided here, and whenever quantities are discussed, this is cited as a comparison. Now, the sands of the Ganges are already immeasurable;
how much more so when one speaks of as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand? Thus, their number is known to be exceedingly vast. [This concludes] the first Great Trichiliocosm of Jewels.
The gift already given was vast; how much more so this gift of jewels filling a great trichiliocosm as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?

Therefore, it is exceedingly great. This concludes the definitive calculation. II. Manifesting Superiority, in two parts: 1. Briefly showing the superiority of the person who maintains [the teaching] and the place;
2. The superiority of the person.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, should even receive, uphold, and recite as few as four lines of verse and explain them to others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."
This is because the Prajñā of Words can express the contemplation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the non-abiding true mind (*amūla-tathatā-citta*).
To "receive" it means to believe and accept this mind; to "uphold" it means to reverently maintain this mind.

By means of these four lines, one awakens to and enters this mind, reveals this mind for all people, and enables both oneself and others to clearly understand this mind. Therefore, this merit is supreme. [The preceding...]

The merit of bestowing material wealth belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, it is inferior. This Dharma-gift, categorized by the four lines [of the verse], belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
therefore, it is superior. It is truly like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold, or a single word of ultimate truth that transforms the ordinary into the holy.

While the many jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have their efficacy in the conditioned—merely bringing retribution in the realms of humans and devas—to briefly uphold this sutra clarifies the mind.
There is no abiding. From this point on, one realizes the nature of reality and possesses the potential for Buddhahood; therefore, this merit surpasses the former merit.
△ Second, the excellence of the location.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place is—
All those in the world—devas, humans, and asuras—should make offerings to this [name] as they would to a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
Regarding these two characters "suishuo" (随说), there are four meanings. First, as for the person who speaks accordingly: there is no distinction made between monastic or lay, ordinary or sage.

Second, following conventional expression regarding meaning, whether the facts or principles be subtle or coarse; third, following conventional expression regarding scriptures, without fixed order of chapters or sentences;
fourth, following conventional expression regarding location, not restricted to cities or mountain forests—know that this applies to all worlds.

This generally encompasses the three realms and the six destinies; herein, only three are mentioned because gods and humans pervade the three realms—whether following or reversing [the flow of saṃsāra]—while asuras are mixed among the four modes of birth, being both substantial and provisional.

All who possess spiritual sentience should obey the Buddha’s command and make offerings at this site to plant supreme causes. Now, the methods of making offerings briefly consist of ten matters: [The text continues with the ten items.]
This refers to offerings of incense, flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, banners, canopies, robes, music, and the joining of palms in prostration.
The Sanskrit term *stūpa* (or *thūpa*) is translated here as "square mound" (*fangfen*), also called "round tomb" (*yuanzong*), or "elevated and prominent place.
The Sanskrit term *caitya* is translated as "sacred shrine" (*lingmiao*). "Shrine" (*miao*) refers to its appearance. [These are] for making offerings.

This is because of the Buddha’s physical form, demeanor, and marks. Now, there are many kinds of stūpas; for now, four shall be mentioned: first, the stūpa of the place of birth; second, the stūpa of the attainment of enlightenment;
third, the stūpa of the turning of the wheel of Dharma; and fourth, the stūpa of parinirvāṇa. Regarding the present instruction on making offerings at these sites:

since these places are themselves the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one should personally receive and transmit the *Prajñāpāramitā* in four lines for the benefit of others, thereby achieving self-benefit.

Benefiting others: for both the speaker and the listener, the enlightened mind and the realization of one's nature—the wondrous essence of the *dharmakāya*—are born from this place where the sutra was heard;
this is the stupa of birth. The *buddhaphala-bodhi* (the fruit of Buddhahood) is accomplished through this place where the sutra was heard; this is the stupa of attaining the Way.
To take even four lines of verse and explain them for others is the stupa of turning the wheel of Dharma. Thus, benefiting oneself and benefiting others is the principle.
The matter is concluded; this is the *parinirvāṇa* stūpa. One should know that wherever the entire sūtra is preached, there is the complete body of the Tathāgata;
wherever it is recited and upheld according to the teaching, there are the relic-śarīras of the fragmented body.

Therefore, the place where the sūtra is preached ought to be treated with reverence, and all humans and devas should make offerings there. △ Second, the superiority of the place where the person who upholds it dwells, in two parts. First:

Such a person would already be superior; how much more so one who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it? Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma.
Even for one who merely recites these four lines according to the teaching, such offerings should still be made;
how much more so for one who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and expound an entire sūtra scroll? Subhūti, you should know that this person accomplishes [the three bodies].

The phrase "accomplishes" (成就) runs through the following text to clarify the meaning of being fully endowed with the three bodies. What does this mean? It is because they accomplish the *dharmakāya*.
The supreme Dharma is untainted and unconditioned, transcending names and severing all marks.
There is not a single dharma that can be added before it, nor is there a single dharma that can surpass it above; therefore, it is called "supreme.
It is the Dharmakāya, which accomplishes the foremost Dharma of the Saṃbhogakāya, adorning itself with myriad virtues and perfecting its marks through a hundred blessings.
Excellent. Among all the holy ones, he is the most honored; there is none superior to him, and thus he is called "the foremost. This is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
He accomplishes the rare dharmas of the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*): appearing as a deva among devas, as a human among humans, as a sheep among sheep, and as a deer among deer.
He divides his form and disperses his shadow, manifesting bodies according to the various classes of beings. Because such wonders are so rare, they are called "rare."
He is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Judging from this, it can be known that he is a person who perfectly possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*), and thus his excellence is evident.
△ Second, the excellence of the place.
Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha and his honored disciples.
Wherever this sutra resides, it is the Dharma Jewel; it is the presence of the Buddha, the True Jewel of the Buddha.
The honored disciples constitute the Sangha Jewel. Thus, the Three Jewels are fully present and completely manifested in one place; such a location—
It is even more evident that [the former] is superior. This comparison to demonstrate superiority necessarily relies on the extensive and concise expositions because the Prajñāpāramitā has two gates:
the extensive and the concise. Since there are two modes of teaching, the same applies to their reception and retention. Furthermore, within these extensive and concise versions...
There must necessarily be self-maintenance and teaching others; this is precisely the intent of entrusting the wealth for the purpose of further instruction. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Among these, whatever is to be taken or given"—this is the summary of that [text], where what is "few" there is "broad" here, and what is "much" there is "brief" here.
Practicing it oneself is "taking," and teaching it to others is "giving. To receive, uphold, read, and recite it is the Buddha’s entrustment.
...wealth. To explain this for others is what the Buddha intends as the turning of the teaching. Following this pattern from beginning to end, there is nothing that does not conform to it.
At this point, the chapter clarifying "bringing down and abiding the mind" is completed. △ Second, manifesting the wondrous function of Prajñā, in two parts.
First, Subhūti requests the name.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named? How should we receive and uphold it?"

When the assembly heard that the sutra existed and the Buddha existed, they recognized its supreme excellence in being upheld and expounded; yet, they did not know its name, nor how it should be received and maintained.
For this reason, they requested its title, as well as the method for its reception and maintenance. Part Two: The Tathāgata’s Instruction (in two sections): 1.
Revealing the Name and Teaching Its Maintenance (in two sections): A. The Formal Designation.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sūtra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this title, you should uphold it.
The meaning of the name established here is that this sūtra represents the function of being free from marks and non-abiding; thus, it takes the diamond (*vajra*) as its metaphor."

If one touches upon existence (*bhava*), then existence is destroyed; if one touches upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then emptiness dissolves; if one touches upon the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), then all things are shattered to pieces.

This is precisely the total clearing away of all phenomena (*dharma*), leaving not even a speck of dust behind; this is what is called the "Vajra. As for that which is called "upholding," there is no separate dharma other than this:
it is nothing more than understanding the meaning through the name and realizing that all phenomena are empty. If, according to...

The Dharma and its metaphor are mentioned together; the Chinese and Sanskrit names are presented side by side. Thus, a detailed explanation of the meaning of these names has already been recorded at the beginning of this scripture and need not be further elaborated here.
Nevertheless, a name is that which calls forth the reality it signifies. Now, let us speak of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Ultimately, what is this? Is it not that which is most firm and most sharp, such that no object can destroy it, yet it is able to destroy all objects?
One might suppose this jewel is used as a metaphor for *prajñā*, which can destroy afflictions (*kleśa*) while the afflictions cannot destroy it—is it indeed this?
Although this may seem close to the truth, I fear it does not quite reach the point. For this...
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is precisely this innate, true mind—free from marks and non-abiding—that each and every person present here possesses.
Therefore, throughout kalpas of cultivation, I, the Tathāgata, have employed this very mind;
in appearing in the world and attaining the Way, I likewise employed this very mind. By employing this mind, one is able to cut through all that cannot otherwise be severed.

Severing that which cannot be let go of—letting it all go completely. Now, having been thoroughly overturned by the one who meets the occasion, with the root and source directly sought out, one can only present the whole dish as it is. But you must recognize this:
you must know that this mind is the very capital for becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor, whether wearing horns or donning fur. If you abandon this mind, there is nothing else.

Dharma. Therefore, I teach you by means of these names; you should uphold them. If you can truly awaken to this mind-dharma, then you will know that the mind is fundamentally no-mind, and dharmas are likewise not-dharmas.
What need is there to speak of the *pāramitās*? They are nothing more than a pair of worn-out straw sandals. As it is said:
"The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to exhaust all minds. If one thoroughly understands all minds, what [need remains]?
Because all dharmas are thus, the Venerable Śāriputra specifically requested the Buddha to extensively point out for all people this one *prajñā* true mind.
Our World-Honored One also requires only that you all uphold this mind;
then the task of study and practice will be complete. I do not yet know whether you can still receive and grasp this mind. Heh! You!
"If there is no mind, I shall simply rest. △ Second, the double explanation:
Why is this so? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls the *prajñāpāramitā* is not [in fact] the *prajñāpāramitā*;
it is merely designated as the *prajñāpāramitā*.

yet they still feel desire upon seeing beautiful forms. How much more so for you, who are in the prime of youth and have not yet severed your lustful desires—how could you see such forms and remain without greed?"
I said, "Great King, that one does not covet forms upon seeing them is truly not due to the practice of *qì* (breath) or the eating of fruits;
it must be due to fixing the mind on impermanence and impurity. The King said, "If one slights others and gives rise to slander, how can they be said to be practicing and upholding the pure precepts?
I said, "I have no anger or envy; why do you say I am slandering? The King asked, "What is called..."
[The King] asked, "What is discipline? He replied, "Patience is called discipline. The King said, "If patience constitutes discipline, I shall cut off your ears;
if you can endure this, I shall know that you uphold discipline. At that time, though my ears were severed, my countenance did not change.
When the king and his ministers saw this, they admonished him, saying, "A great being such as this should not be subjected to harm. The King asked, "How do you know he is a great being?"

The ministers said, "When he was seen undergoing such suffering, his countenance did not change. The King said, "I shall test him further," and immediately cut off his nose and severed his hands and feet.

At that time, throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, I had cultivated loving-kindness and compassion, feeling pity for suffering sentient beings with a heart free from anger or resentment. Then the Four Heavenly Kings, harboring wrath and indignation, rained down sand.
There were pebbles and stones. Upon seeing this, the king was greatly terrified. He came to me once more, knelt down for a long time, and said:
"I only pray that you will have compassion and grant me permission to repent. I said: "Great King, my mind is free from anger, just as it is free from greed. The king said: "Virtuous One..."

"How can this be known? I then made a vow: 'If it is true that I am free from anger and resentment, may this body be restored to its former state. Having made this aspiration, my body was immediately restored.
I further prayed that in a future life I might attain bodhi and first deliver the Great King; therefore, having now become a Buddha, I have delivered Kauṇḍinya. Thus it was I.
This forbearance did not stop with King Kali alone. Furthermore, he recalled that during five hundred lifetimes, he had been a great seer named Śāntivādin (Proponent of Forbearance).
Throughout all those worlds, he was entirely free from the four marks [of self, person, being, and life]; thus, his forbearance was so habitual that he regarded it as something ordinary.
One should know that forbearance devoid of the four marks is the foremost *pāramitā*. If one lacks wisdom, [forbearance is merely mundane].
Thus, one cannot remain free from resentment; even if one endures it for a single moment, one cannot endure it through many lifetimes.

Even if one willingly accepts such suffering, one still cannot move the king [of the Dharma]. This is why the World-Honored One, in elucidating the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) through the revelation of the signless (*animitta*), truly feared that "speaking of food would not satisfy the hunger. He desired that those present at the assembly personally taste a single mouthful.
△ Fifth, the conclusion on the characteristic of detachment:
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while remaining detached from all characteristics.

Having already completed the preceding seal of approval and exposition, he here concludes with an exhortation, saying: "A bodhisattva should, as I have done above, resolve upon bodhicitta while remaining free from signs;
they must also necessarily cultivate this practice of being free from signs. Thus, these two characters [refer to the aforementioned].
This concludes the preceding section. It refers specifically to what you asked me previously: "Good sons and good daughters, how should they resolve their minds?
How should they abide? Therefore, you should know that a Bodhisattva who studies Prajñāpāramitā ought to resolve their mind by way of detachment from signs (*animitta*).
Herein, the Buddha reveals the function of detachment from signs, as well as the preceding stages of abiding and resolving the mind.
The principle that the mind has no dharma is laid bare in its entirety. Yet, although the interlocutor heard this teaching, he failed to reflect deeply;
it is a pity that he missed the point right before his eyes. Therefore, he subsequently asked: "How does one subdue the arising of the thought of enlightenment?
Had he realized the principle that the thought of enlightenment has no dharma at this point, then the latter half [of the text]...

The questions and answers in this fascicle may now be concluded. To greedily gaze at the waves before one’s eyes while losing the oar in one’s hand—this is precisely what is meant by "the opportune moment" (*dangji*).
This concludes the manifestation of the function of *prajñā* as being free from marks (*lixiang*). △ Second, the manifestation of the function of *prajñā* as non-abiding (*wuzhu*), in two parts.
First, the direct clarification of non-abiding, in three parts. First, not abiding in the six sense-objects (*liuchen*).
One should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
If the mind has a dwelling, it is not a true dwelling. Therefore, the Buddha said that a bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on forms when practicing giving.
Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.
This concludes the preceding discussion on dwelling in the mind through both detailed and abbreviated explanations of non-dwelling, thereby manifesting the non-abiding function of Prajñā.
Although non-dwelling was previously elucidated through sequential explanation, direct clarification, illustrative metaphor, and comparative analysis, it is here brought to its definitive conclusion.
Previously, before the "binding" (the formal conclusion) had occurred, the function of the markless (*animitta*) was discussed.
Now that the binding of the markless function has been completed, we shall here bind the function of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*). This is precisely the formal conclusion of the preceding passage:

"One should practice giving while having nothing to which one abides," as well as "one should give rise to the mind while having nothing to which one abides. "Should not" refers to the aforementioned "should."
"No" is also a term of admonition. What is meant here by "one should not give rise to the mind" is that the mind is fundamentally unborn;

it arises only because of external objects. Therefore, to give rise to the mind is delusion, and to stir a thought is to deviate from the truth. One must not dwell upon or become attached to the six sense-objects.
When one practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), this demonstrates the principle of non-abiding. One should give rise to a state of non-abiding.
"Your mind should, precisely, arise without abiding anywhere. This exhorts one to realize the principle of non-abiding.

For the aforementioned arising of the mind while abiding in form and so forth is the deluded mind; whereas the subsequent instruction to "arise with a mind that abides nowhere" refers to the true mind.
This is the true mind. Therefore, the two characters "should not" (bù yīng) are used to admonish you not to dwell;
the character "should" (yīng) is used to exhort you that [the mind] ought to arise. If the mind dwells, it is precisely non-dwelling.
This clarifies the intent behind my teaching that you should not dwell: should your mind have even a single point of attachment, it immediately belongs to the illusory consciousness of delusion.
It is not, however, the true mind that is non-abiding. This clearly demonstrates that abiding in [phenomena] deviates from the essence of the Dharma;
it is not the principle of the non-abiding real-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, the ancient masters said: "To turn away from objects is superior; to pursue objects is inferior.
The moment a subtle emotion arises, one immediately falls to the ground. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* correctly states: "If one can master objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata. This...
This is what is meant. Therefore, below, it demonstrates the emptiness of the three wheels. "One should practice giving without dwelling on form" refers to the emptiness of the giver.
"For the sake of benefiting sentient beings" refers to the emptiness of the recipient. "One should practice giving in this manner" [refers to the emptiness of the act of giving].
This refers back to the meaning of "non-abiding" mentioned above. Internally, one does not abide in a self; externally, one does not abide in a person;
and in between, one does not abide in the object to be given—this is the emptiness of the gift.
Thus, all three spheres are empty, which can truly be called the practice of giving without abiding. This clarifies that a Bodhisattva’s practice of giving should not...

Abiding in attachment was originally intended for the benefit of sentient beings. However, if there is even the slightest attachment, it means that the distinction between self and others has not been forgotten, thereby creating conditions of hatred and love with sentient beings.

If this is the case, then throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, one will be mutually related as children, grandchildren, parents, or enemies and creditors; with resentment and gratitude entangled, how could one ever escape the cycle of birth and death?
Liberation. For this reason, when practicing the giving of alms, one must not abide in the six sense objects while giving.
If one can practice giving in this manner, it constitutes "non-abiding" giving and is an outflow-free field of merit.
This is why the Tathāgata’s teaching that people must never abide in signs when practicing giving is indeed for a profound reason. △ Two.
One does not dwell in persons or dharmas.
The Tathāgata has said that all marks are indeed no-marks; he has also said that all sentient beings are indeed no-sentient-beings.
To summarize the foregoing: by practicing patience and giving, one manifests the meaning of non-abiding.

To say that all marks are, in fact, no-marks precisely reveals the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness)—which is neither with marks, nor without marks, nor not-without-marks, nor not-not-without-marks, nor both with and without marks, nor a single mark, nor diverse marks, nor not [any of these].

It is the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). It is not the characteristic of non-difference; it is not the characteristic of both unity and difference. Rather, it is the true characteristic of emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*).

Furthermore, when it is said that "all sentient beings are themselves not sentient beings," it is because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions and have falsely identified the four great elements as their own self-characteristic and the six sense-objects as...
The shadow is but a manifestation of one's own mind. Thus, through the conjunction of the four great elements, the five aggregates, and the six sense objects, the various phenomena arise;

these are conventionally designated as "sentient beings. If one were to dissect the skin, flesh, and ribs so that they return to earth, the semen, fluids, phlegm, and saliva so that they return to water, the warmth so that it returns to fire, and the movements so that they return to wind—tell me, where does this delusory body reside? Within these, there are the six sense objects.

Each returns to dispersion and extinction; ultimately, no mind with conditions can be perceived. Even if one were separated from the four great elements, the five aggregates, and the six sense objects, no sentient being could be found.
Therefore, it is said: "It is not a sentient being. This is because the aforementioned various marks are non-marks, meaning that all phenomena are empty.
Thus, one is far removed from attachment to both phenomena and non-phenomena. As for the sentient beings mentioned below...
"Non-arising" means that both persons and dharmas are empty; thus, one remains far removed from the grasping at a self.

If this is correlated with the meaning of the preceding chapter, it is precisely the emptiness and stillness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), wherein the three types of grasping are dissolved and the three kinds of emptiness are manifested.
This is the non-abiding function of Prajñāpāramitā, which may be said to be most clearly and manifestly evident. △ Third, the conclusion that reveals the reality, in two parts. First:
This clearly elucidates the ultimate reality:
"Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks what is real, one who speaks according to suchness, one who does not speak deceptively,
and one who does not speak otherwise."
This concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one, exhorting the reader to generate faith and understanding and to practice accordingly.

Because of the various characteristics explained above—namely, that they are "not-characteristics" and that sentient beings are "not-sentient-beings"—one might fear thinking: "The Bodhisattva acts for the benefit of all sentient beings;

why then is it said here again that sentient beings are not sentient beings? Is this not a contradiction between emptiness and existence? Is it not inconsistent? To address such doubts, [the text continues].
Therefore it is said: "The Tathāgata is one who speaks the true word and the real word. This clarifies that there is no doubt or error for future students;
it is as when it is said, "The Buddha taught the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), which is truly and without exception such.

Furthermore, when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he necessarily accords with principle and accords with the capacities [of beings]. Whatever he says all returns to the principle of the Three Truths (tri-satya). As for what is called the "true word":

"Truthful speech" refers to speaking in accordance with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Real speech" refers to speaking in accordance with the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) and the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"Non-deceptive and non-different" refers to speaking in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) for the present time.
Furthermore, "truthful speech" means being without falsehood; "real speech" means being without vanity; and "truthful speech" means being in accord with what has been realized.
Thus it is said. "Not different" means there is no further alteration or change. The Wei translation contains only these four phrases;
however, Master Kumārajīva’s version contains five. This is likely because he followed the treatise of Vasubandhu, wishing to encompass the four phrases in order to elucidate the Buddha’s intent:
that each and every thing is real and not false. For this reason, one must have faith.
These are my sincere words; I do not deceive you. II. A further explanation of the ultimate truth:
Subhūti, as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
This correctly upholds the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words as being true. For because this Dharma is without substantiality, it is said that sentient beings are not sentient beings;
and because this Dharma is without falsehood, it is said to benefit all sentient beings.
Thus, everything spoken by the Tathāgata accords with principle and is entirely true; it is not deceptive or otherwise. This is precisely...
This establishes the practice of giving without abiding, teaching that one must not dwell in attachment. Why?

Because this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is unlike the dharmas of the aggregates, bases, and elements grasped by worldly people—which are either real or unreal—whereas this is neither real nor unreal.
Because it is not real, its wondrous existence is non-existent; because it is not...
Because it is empty, true emptiness is not empty; because it exists as wondrous being, it does not exist. Therefore, one does not abide in existent phenomena.
Thus, the marks of the body are not marks of the body; enlightenment is not enlightenment; the preaching of the Dharma is not the preaching of the Dharma; and the world is not the world.
Atoms are not atoms; adornments are not adornments, and so forth. Because they are based on emptiness that is not empty, one does not abide in non-dharmas.

Therefore, these are called the marks of the body, called bodhi, called the teaching of the Dharma, called the world, called atoms, and called adornments, and so forth. Since these lack substantial reality, one does not abide in existence.
Because this is not empty, one does not abide in emptiness. Contemplating the Buddha’s discourse on true emptiness and wondrous existence serves to manifest the non-abiding function of *prajñā*.
Reaching this point, it may be said that [the teaching] is exhausted with nothing remaining.
△ Second, illustrating the function through analogies, in two parts: First, presenting the analogy, in two parts: First, the analogy that abiding is not subtle.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with a mind attached to phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.

This is a metaphor for the fault of dwelling upon signs (*nimitta*). It was because the World-Honored One feared that the disciple might not be able to suddenly empty the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) that he spoke thus.
It still retains a trace of ambiguity; therefore, an analogy is raised to clarify the fault of the mark of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) being suboptimal.

It is said that when a Bodhisattva’s mind dwells upon marks while practicing giving, not only is it unable to transcend the sense bases and their objects (*āyatana*), but it is moreover turned by external things.
On the contrary, they are shrouded by greed and ignorance, merely increasing the conditions for hatred and attachment.
Thus, one who practices giving while unable to attain the wondrous function of non-abiding prajñā encounters obstacles at every turn. It is like a pair of fine eyes entering a dark room;
even if there were immeasurable treasures within the house, one could not see them. How, then, could one enjoy their use?
△ Second, the analogy that non-abiding is supreme:
If a bodhisattva’s mind does not abide in phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person with eyes who, when the sun shines with light,
sees all manner of forms.
This is a metaphor for the merit of non-abiding. For if one abides, one is entangled by external objects;

if one does not abide, one is immediately able to transform things, sweeping away the three attachments and thoroughly realizing the three voids. Only then can it be said that the great function of the Vajra has manifested before one.
Only then can the obscurations of emotion melt away like ice, and the light of wisdom shine in perfect clarity. When viewed through the eye of the Way, every phenomenon is luminous.

Illumination is like a person who possesses eyes; when further added to by the shining light of the sun, they are able to see all manner of forms and colors in their entirety. This is what is meant by "not a single thread of silk hanging" and "ten thousand *li* without a cloud. One strikes open the pivot and personally beholds the original person. As for this function of non-abiding, nothing can surpass its wondrousness. Thus, it is said: [The text continues with the verse: ...the mind is originally bright and clear, Like the moon reflected in the water. When the clouds suddenly disperse, The sky is naturally vast and open. If one does not seek elsewhere, How could there be any obstruction? The myriad phenomena are all within, Yet they do not obstruct one another. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not look at the ten directions. If you look at the ten directions, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own face. If you look at your own face, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the scriptures. If you seek it in the scriptures, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own mind. If you look at your own mind, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the body. If you seek it in the body, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own nature. If you look at your own nature, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the senses. If you seek it in the senses, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own essence. If you look at your own essence, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the mind. If you seek it in the mind, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own source. If you look at your own source, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the thoughts. If you seek it in the thoughts, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own root. If you look at your own root, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the consciousnesses. If you seek it in the consciousnesses, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own ground. If you look at your own ground, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the dharmas. If you seek it in the dharmas, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own reality. If you look at your own reality, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the teachings. If you seek it in the teachings, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own wisdom. If you look at your own wisdom, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the practice. If you seek it in the practice, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own realization. If you look at your own realization, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the path. If you seek it in the path, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own attainment. If you look at your own attainment, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the fruit. If you seek it in the fruit, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own liberation. If you look at your own liberation, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the vows. If you seek it in the vows, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own compassion. If you look at your own compassion, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the precepts. If you seek it in the precepts, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own morality. If you look at your own morality, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own devotion. If you look at your own devotion, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the merit. If you seek it in the merit, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own virtue. If you look at your own virtue, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the dhyāna. If you seek it in the dhyāna, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own samādhi. If you look at your own samādhi, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the prajñā. If you seek it in the prajñā, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own insight. If you look at your own insight, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the liberation. If you seek it in the liberation, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own nirvāṇa. If you look at your own nirvāṇa, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the emptiness. If you seek it in the emptiness, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own non-arising. If you look at your own non-arising, You will immediately see it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Do not seek it in the signlessness. If you seek it in the signlessness, You will never find it. If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, Look directly at your own wishlessness. If you look at your own wishlessness, You will immediately see it.
