O Bodhisattva of the Mind, can you not seek deeply into non-abiding? △ Second, the manifestation of function, which has two parts: first, the function of generating merit;
second, the merit of self-benefit.
Subhūti, in future ages, if there are good men or good women who are able, regarding this sutra, to receive...
If one upholds, reads, and recites it, the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, fully knows this person and fully sees this person;
all shall achieve immeasurable and boundless merit.
The preceding section used five statements and two metaphors to testify to and exhort the practice of non-abiding generosity (*apratisthita-dāna*).

Now that the practitioner has attained the stillness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), eliminated the three attachments, and manifested the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā*), the intent of this sutra may be said to be profound indeed.
Yet, as the merit of upholding this sutra has not yet been recognized, it is now revealed here. This is because the future age will precisely correspond to this time. What follows...

This means that those who are turbid and evil are many, while those who receive the Way are few. Unless one has long planted roots of goodness, one cannot receive, uphold, read, or recite [this teaching].
That it is said here that one "can" do so does not merely refer to the ability to recite words, phrases, and sentences;

it also refers to the ability to receive and uphold the wondrous meaning of non-abiding. Thus, the merit of such a person cannot be matched even by the provisional vehicles or their minor fruits. Therefore, it is said:
This means that the Tathāgata, by means of his Buddha-wisdom, knows all and sees all. This is what constitutes "this" [in the phrase "this is for him"].

It should be understood as the character *de* (to obtain), meaning that he immediately attains resonance and response. Regarding "by means of Buddha-wisdom," "knows all" refers to the Buddha’s threefold penetration (*trividya*) illuminating everything;
"sees all" refers to the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) observing perfectly. The phrase "such as this" points back to what preceded.
In the chapter on the extensive and the concise, it describes the merit of immeasurable space and boundless worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Question:
Throughout the beginning and end of this sutra, there are repeated comparisons and evaluations; what is the Buddha’s underlying intent? Answer:

It is because the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is the unattached, true doctrine, truly a secret scripture for sealing the mind and the authentic explanation for entering the state of sainthood. [Those who] cling to the three [aspects] as empty are deluded...

The mind finds rest; the three wisdoms manifest, and the true reality (*dharmatā*) is perfected. If one's contemplation is not slightly refined and pure, how can the mind become empty and the environment tranquil?
Without relying on the *prajñā* of words and letters, by what means could one recognize the path and return home?

Therefore, in all instances of formal realization, the merit of upholding and expounding [the Dharma] is extensively clarified, no more than to ensure that the lineage of the Way flows perpetually and that the Dharma...
Its source is inexhaustible; its subtle words shall not perish. The intent lies herein. △ Second, the merit of benefiting others, in two parts.
First, a brief explanation of the merit:
"Subhūti, if there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, [sacrificed] bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."

During the middle part of the day, he again gives away as many bodies as there are sands in the Ganges River; during the latter part of the day, he likewise gives away as many bodies as there are sands in the Ganges River.
In this manner, he gives away his body for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Yet, if there should be another person who, upon hearing this sutra, believes it with faith and does not reject it, their merit would surpass that of the former; how much more so if they were to copy, receive, and uphold it?
"Uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others. Subhūti, to speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he has taught it for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle."
This comparison of the merit of upholding and reciting [the Prajñāpāramitā] against that of giving one's own body serves to manifest the power of non-abiding in the Prajñā.

Generally, a day is divided into three parts: the first part consists of the hours of Chén and Sì; the middle part consists of the hours of Wǔ and Wèi; and the latter part consists of the hours of Shēn and Yǒu.
This refers to three periods each day, in which one gives away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
this may be called the diligence of practicing *dāna*. Yet, it does not stop at one or two days;

rather, such days accumulate into eons (*kalpa*), from one to a hundred, until reaching immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. This is an extreme way of describing its duration. And...

How much more so when, for three periods every day, one practices giving with bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges? This is the gift of internal wealth (*ādhyātmika-dāna*), and its merit is naturally immeasurable.

*Kalpa* in Sanskrit is translated here as "long duration. There are small, medium, and great *kalpas*, differing according to the analogies of the mustard-seed city, the wiping of a stone, and the increments and decrements [of the cosmic cycle].
The above has been used to determine the superiority of this merit; yet even so, it does not equal [the merit of the former].
To hear this sutra, the meaning of the non-abiding Prajñā, with even a single thought of faith—this is what is meant by "not being contrary.
To speak contrarily is to commit an act of defiance; it is what is called slandering the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) scriptures.

Conversely, to say one is not contrary means to accord with this Prajñā of letters, the meaning of non-abiding, and not to give rise to slander. The merit of this alone already surpasses that of giving away one's own body.

How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and explain it for others. This receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting constitutes self-benefit; explaining it for others constitutes benefit for others.
It clearly demonstrates that even hearing it once and believing and following it brings merit that surpasses the gift of one's own body as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
How much more so for one who possesses both benefits? The merit of such a person is all the more difficult to compare. This is because...
It is necessary to summarize. At first, one compares the few with the many, yet it is difficult to match their excellence. Now, proceeding from the extensive to the essential, it is said:
"To state it briefly. This means that even if one were to provide a complete eulogy, it could never be exhausted;
yet even when speaking briefly, there is that which cannot be conceived by the mind, cannot be discussed in words, and cannot be measured by quantity or described in terms of length.

Its measure is truly boundless and limitless in its merit. One should know that although such internal giving involves great matters and long durations, the resulting blessings are still contaminated (*sāsrava*).
However, if one can accord with *prajñā*, then both self and others will be benefited.
The realization of the fruit of Bodhi is the merit of this untainted Dharma-gift; how could it be measured by means of a tainted body subject to birth and death?

The Tathāgata spoke thus to encourage those below and support those above, saying that this sutra possesses inconceivable merit because it was taught for those who have resolved their minds toward the Mahāyāna and for those who have resolved their minds toward the Supreme Vehicle.

Regarding the mind, it is so designated because it is taught as such. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, its greatness is threefold, namely: essence (*tǐ*), characteristics (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*).
Furthermore, fearing that this might be confused with provisional teachings, it is distinguished by the "Supreme Vehicle," which is the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).

While the Mahāyāna generally encompasses those of gradual capacity who turn back from the small toward the great, the Supreme Vehicle refers to those who do not pass through successive stages but are perfected [from the outset].
This person is one of sudden enlightenment. △ Second, the detailed explanation of merit has three parts. First, the actual clarification of the merit of the detailed exposition:
If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this for others, the Tathāgata fully knows this person and fully sees this person;
all shall achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Virtue. Such persons as these are indeed those who shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is an extensive exposition on the exhortation to uphold [the teaching] in order to manifest its merit; that is to say, since this sutra is taught for the sake of Mahāyāna practitioners.
However, one who is able to receive, uphold, and extensively expound [the Dharma], possessing the virtues of the two benefits, is likewise a person of the Mahāyāna.
As for "extensively expounding," it refers not merely to a single or two individuals, nor merely to four lines of verse;
rather, it means establishing the great banner of the Dharma amidst a vast assembly of people and universally bestowing the rain of the *prajñā* Dharma. Thus, then—
The merit of this person cannot be fathomed by the mind nor proclaimed by the mouth; only the Tathāgata can fully know and see it.

From those below him, none are able to recognize it. Why is this? Because this person, being able to benefit both themselves and others, is one who carries upon their back the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata. To carry on the back is to bear a burden. On...
The shoulders serve as the burden. This means that only those who possess these two kinds of benefit are capable of bearing heavy responsibility and traveling great distances;
they are the ones who shoulder the burden for the Buddha and act on his behalf in practicing the Way. △ Second, the contrastive revelation of the inability of those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle.
Why is this? Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span;
they are thus unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sūtra to others.
This is an implicit demonstration by way of contrast. It clarifies that those who are unable to take up the responsibility of *prajñā* are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Question: The Buddha-mind is impartial, and its bestowal of the Dharma is likewise so. Why, then, was it stated above that [this teaching] is intended solely for the Mahāyāna?

"Is it for those of the Supreme Vehicle? He replied: "Those who delight in the Lesser [Vehicle] are unable themselves to hear, believe, accept, or uphold [the Mahāyāna]; this has been explained at length.
That is to say, they consider the price of a single day to be a great gain; how could they find leisure to set their minds upon the Great Jewel of the Dharma King?

This is because those who delight in the Lesser have not yet emptied the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), have not yet eliminated attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*), and take pleasure in the Lesser."

Consequently, being attached to signs and arrogant, indulging in falsehoods and deeply clinging to them without relinquishing them, how could they be willing to listen to or believe this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra regarding the meaning of detachment from signs and non-abiding?
Moreover, if they cannot even listen to or believe it, how could they possibly uphold, recite, or extensively explain its essential meaning to others? This is precisely so.
It was because they were of limited capacity that they could not possibly receive, uphold, or explain it extensively.
Now, since you are able to listen to, receive, read, recite, and explain it for others, you are not comparable to those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle.

How can you not be called Mahāyāna practitioners, supreme vehicle practitioners, and those who shoulder the burden of Bodhi? △ Third, the conclusion: pointing to the location of the sutra, one should make offerings.
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be, it should be honored by all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it with reverence.
With various flowers and incense, one should scatter them over that place;
this exhorts the protectors of the Dharma to make offerings to the sutra. "Wherever" (xūxūbōti xià) means wherever the sutra is located;

"in every place" (chùchù) refers to the places where the sutra resides. All of these summarize what was previously stated in the chapter on Non-Abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*). "According to the teaching" (suíshuō).
One should know that this sutra—even if it consists of only four lines—should be venerated by all devas and humans at that place as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
To speak of "reverence" means to prostrate and circumambulate; to speak of "respect" means to offer various incenses, flowers, and so forth.
This expresses reverence through both the primary [Dharma] and the secondary [relics]. A stupa is where the relics of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) are enshrined.
Furthermore, this scripture is the repository for the *dharmakāya* relics; therefore, it is all the more fitting that it be venerated. Question:

Since this has already been stated previously, why is it repeated here? Answer: The previous passage clarified the meaning of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*), stating that the scripture, its location, and the person [who transmits it] should all be venerated.
This present passage clarifies the wondrous function of non-abiding; how could it not be so regarding the scripture, its location, and the person?
Ah! Furthermore, it was previously stated, "like a Buddha’s stūpa or temple," whereas here it says, "this is itself the stūpa. The term "itself" (ji) is more intimate than "like" (ru).
Since the textual expressions and their meanings differ, they are not redundant. △ Second, the function of extinguishing transgressions has three parts.
First, the explicit explanation of the wondrous function of extinguishing transgressions.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds, recites, and studies this sutra, yet is treated with contempt by others,
their karmic offenses from previous lives— which would otherwise have caused them to fall into the evil realms—
are extinguished by virtue of being so treated with contempt in the present life. They shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This reveals that there are two inconceivable aspects to the practice of upholding and reciting [this sutra]. First, by treating what is light as heavy, one is able to transform fixed karma;
thus, the retribution is inconceivable. Second, one shall attain bodhi; thus, the fruit is inconceivable.
This explains the doubt that one might not obtain supreme merit from upholding the sutra. Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Subhūti," it says:

Since this sutra is taught for the sake of those who have set forth upon the Mahāyāna and the Supreme Vehicle, and since those who uphold and expound it possess inconceivable merit, wherever this sutra resides is itself a stūpa of the Buddha;
thus, all devas and humans should pay it reverence. These are the true and sincere words of the Tathāgata, and they are certainly to be believed. How could it be otherwise?

There are currently good men and good women who, while upholding, receiving, reading, and reciting [this teaching] therein, not only fail to receive the respect of humans and devas, but are instead treated with contempt by the world. Why is this? What is meant by "contempt" is that they are not held in high regard;
what is meant by "contemptuous treatment" is that they are not honored. Now, such instances of contemptuous treatment are of many kinds: some arise from the practice of jealousy, or...
They harbor resentment and suspicion; some slander him out of anger, while others bully him by relying on their power.

In extreme cases, they even assault him with blades, staves, tiles, stones, fists, or feet—all acts of contempt. Observing this, one might ask: "Wherein lies the merit of the sutra? Śākyamuni replied:
"This is due to the person's karmic offenses from previous lives. It is because that person did not yet recognize the Buddha and had not yet heard [the Dharma]."
At a time when the Dharma has not yet appeared, when one has not yet encountered the Sangha, and when one has not yet upheld the Prajñāpāramitā, do not speak of this person’s many past lives.
Even regarding this present life, how can one guarantee that during the first half of it they performed only meritorious deeds and committed no sinful karma?
Since sinful karma exists, in future lives they will surely fall into the evil realms and suffer without end.
"Exhaustion" refers to the evil realms, namely the three evil paths: hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Now, by virtue of upholding this sutra, one transforms heavy retribution into light retribution, and transforms retribution to be experienced in future lives or subsequent lives so that it is experienced in the present.
Because one is currently treated with contempt by others, the karmic offenses committed in previous lives are thereby extinguished through this means.
It is extinguished; one shall no longer fall back into the three miserable realms. Is this not the extraordinary merit of Prajñā?
Moreover, it does not merely extinguish transgressions; by practicing this, one shall attain Buddhahood. Therefore, it is said: "One shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The term "shall attain" precisely means that although one does not attain it now, one will certainly attain it in the future.
How could one, because of being slighted or despised by others, conclude that the practice of recitation is without merit?

Observing it from this perspective, one should further realize the wondrous efficacy of this sutra in transforming karmic retribution and attaining the fruit of Buddhahood. △ Second, concurrently revealing the wondrous efficacy of the sutra’s merit.
Subhūti, I recall that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
I encountered eight hundred and forty million nayutas of Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, none of whom I failed to honor.
If there should be anyone in the future final age who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they shall obtain—
Compared to the merit of my making offerings to all the Buddhas, it does not equal even one hundredth part; it does not equal one ten-millionth, one billionth, or even one trillionth part;
indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.
This reveals that the wondrous efficacy of the sutra’s merit is inconceivable. From the passage beginning with "Subhūti," the text proceeds to compare merit with wisdom.
"I" refers to the true self of the Dharma-body; "recollection" (nian) refers to clear calculation and non-forgetfulness.
"Asaṃkhyeya" translates as "innumerable"; it is one of the ten great numerical units. However, it is called "immeasurable asaṃkhyeya."
This refers to the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Indeed, our World-Honored One, while formerly serving as the potter Viśvabhū, encountered the ancient Śākyamuni, who guided him and inspired his resolve;
he then cultivated the path toward the fruit of Buddhahood until the first *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa was completed.

Upon meeting the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, the second *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa was completed. Upon meeting the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the third *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa was completed. Upon meeting the Tathāgata Vipaśyin...
"Come. As for the current statement, "prior to Ratnaprabhāsa," this refers to the period before he had yet seen Ratnaprabhāsa.
*Nayuta* is the ninth numerical unit; numerically, it equals ten million. "Making offerings" refers to the four requisites.

"Attending upon" means to personally serve and attend to them, following their instructions without transgression. Regarding "not passing by in vain": as mentioned above, [the Bodhisattva] never passed by even a single Buddha in vain.

Yet they do not offer worship or serve them. This refers precisely to the World-Honored One himself, who, during his own causal stage, made offerings to so many Buddhas that not a single one passed by in vain; the merit of such deeds is truly immeasurable.
If compared with those who uphold this sutra in the final age, it does not equal even a fraction of the latter. Why is this? Because while making offerings to the Buddhas—
Matters belonging to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are conceivable; however, the merit of upholding the *Prajñāpāramitā* belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and is therefore inconceivable.
Thus, how could one ever fully describe the wondrous efficacy of this sūtra’s merit? △ Third, a summary of the sūtra’s merit and wondrous efficacy.
Subhūti, if good sons or good daughters, in the final age at the end of time, should receive, uphold, read,
and recite this sutra, the merit they would obtain— if I were to describe it in full— some who hear it might have their minds become deranged or fall into doubt and lack faith.
Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
Commentary:
This concludes the two preceding chapters on "Transcending Characteristics" and "Non-abiding" to clarify the nature of the fruition and retribution.
The meaning of the sutra is entirely inconceivable. This precisely refers to what I have said above regarding the sons of good family and others—that such comparisons do not suffice.
The merits [of this] have been described only briefly; were they explained in full detail, I fear people would find it difficult to believe and might instead give rise to doubt.
As for the term "fox," it refers to a sly beast, namely the jackal (*śṛgāla*). Its nature is one of much suspicion; when crossing a frozen river in winter, it walks while listening.
If there is no sound of water flowing beneath the ice, it proceeds; if there is a sound, it retreats. Because of this—
The progression and regression are not uniform; this is used as a metaphor for those who harbor doubts. This is called the "Superior Merit of Prajñā.

Those of inferior faculties may not yet hear it in its entirety, for there is fear that they might become deranged or fall into disbelief, thereby incurring the transgression of slandering the Dharma.
Therefore, only a small portion is spoken here. Why is this? Because the principles of this sutra clarify the true mark (*dharmatā*), the mark-free, and the non-abiding true mind.

It is profoundly deep and inconceivable; the retributive fruits obtained by those who uphold it belong entirely to the untainted and unsurpassed, and are therefore beyond the reach of thought or deliberation.
Thus, the scriptural text concludes this section by evaluating five successive stages.

Twice with external wealth, twice with internal giving—this constitutes one instance of the causes for Buddhahood. Having reached this point, the comparison is exhaustive and can no longer be extended;
hence it is said: "even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy. One must understand the subsequent passage.

Although there are comparisons made, they are merely cited according to the circumstances at hand—whether it be the treasures of a single trichiliocosm, or a heap of jewels like Mount Sumeru, or the treasures of incalculable worlds (asaṃkhyeya-loka-dhātu)—none of these equal those mentioned in the preceding text. There are two reasons for this:
first, it is feared that those of shallow understanding, upon hearing such things, would find them difficult to believe and accept, thereby leading to slander and defamation.

Regarding the offenses: as for the second point, since they have already been extensively compared within the two preceding chapters on "Detachment from Characteristics" and "Non-abiding," the greatness of the merit of the subsequent "Dharma-less Resolve" can be known by analogy.

Although it does not follow the same sequence of shallow and deep as the former, its meaning is even more profound; for the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise so.

It is inconceivable, yet it governs all. Thus, by means of the "Foremost Head," the method for subduing and stabilizing the mind has been shown. This concludes the detailed exposition of the wondrous functions of Prajñā.
*Commentary on the Heart Seal of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume One.
