△ Second, clarifying that there is no dharma in Bodhi, thereby correctly revealing the fundamental essence of Prajñā, in three parts: First, the correct elucidation of Bodhi.
The Two Methods of Inquiry. First, the inquiry prompted by the occasion.

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?"

This question concerns the initial arousal of the bodhicitta. Truly, one who wishes to arouse the bodhicitta must first subdue delusive thoughts and attachments, and abide securely in the non-abiding true mind of prajñā; only then will it be stable and appropriate.
Were it otherwise, this deluded mind would remain unsubdued, grasping at objects everywhere and becoming stained by attachment at every turn.
This would then be in direct contradiction with the principle of non-abiding. Therefore, the World-Honored One first answered regarding subduing [the mind], and subsequently clarified abiding;
his intention was that if one can truly abide in non-abiding, then the mind of deluded thought and attachment—
Without waiting for subjugation, one is spontaneously subdued. If this is so, then the settling of the mind is complete, and the realization of the Way can be achieved.

Therefore, although the various preceding examinations have progressively elucidated the principle of non-abiding free from characteristics, they have not yet explained how the bodhicitta is generated, nor how the unsurpassed Way is realized.
When the practitioner reaches this point, they receive the Buddha’s instruction to transcend all marks while delivering sentient beings and to practice giving without abiding.

Thus, those who have not yet been subdued are subdued, and those who have not yet attained stability are stabilized. Yet, they still do not know whether the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* has actually been produced or not produced;
nor do they know whether the path of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment has actually been accomplished or not.
Is it so? For this reason, I have raised this question. My intention was that when I previously asked, "How should a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon Bodhicitta abide?

How should they subdue [the mind]?"—having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction on the meaning of abiding and subduing, I have already attained faith and understanding. However, regarding the meaning of the initial resolution itself, I have not yet [fully grasped it].
Illumination. I humbly beseech the Tathāgata not to withhold his instructions, but to grant me a further explanation.
This will enable these men and women of virtuous faith from this day forward to readily resolve their minds toward the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and practice its realization.
△ Second, the World-Honored One’s direct response (in three parts). First, he follows the previous section by abiding in the descent of non-dharmas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
'I should bring all sentient beings to final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*).
Yet, after having brought all sentient beings to final liberation, not a single sentient being has actually been liberated. Why is this? Subhūti, if..."
If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.

This follows upon the previous section on "subduing and abiding," serving as the introduction to the answer regarding the non-existence of the dharma of generating the aspiration for enlightenment. As for the character "者" (zhě):
This refers to the person who has resolved their mind [for enlightenment]. "The arising of that which is to arise" means the arising of the very act of generating the resolve.

Regarding this "mind": it refers back to what precedes and points forward to what follows. To refer back: it points back to the preceding passage on practicing giving without dwelling, as well as the instruction, "one should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere.

It is also the mind that should generate the mind of non-dwelling. For the Buddha’s intention was this: *Note: The original text contains a complex layering of grammatical reference (anaphora and cataphora) regarding the term "mind" (心). The translation reflects this by using "the mind" for the primary subject and "the mind that should generate... to capture the reflexive nature of the original Chinese syntax.*
This principle has already been clarified; why then ask again? Moreover, I have already stated that a bodhisattva should abide only as instructed.
One who resolves their mind [on awakening] should give rise to such a non-abiding mind; this is precisely the mind of bodhi.
This is to dwell in non-dwelling; to dwell without dwelling is precisely true dwelling. Since the mind has no dwelling, how could dharmas have any reality?
That the dharma is without dwelling is exactly what it is like. Pointing downward refers to the method for subduing the mind.

It is merely the practice of saving sentient beings while remaining free from attachment to signs. One must understand that this section specifically clarifies the Bodhisattva’s mind of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.
The non-abiding practice of giving and so forth is the "seeking above," while this saving of beings through detachment from signs is the "transforming below.
As the Sūtra says: "I should bring all sentient beings to extinction [of suffering]," and so on. This is precisely...
This refers to the task of transforming those below. The two characters "I" (吾) and "should" (應) signify that one is taught to take the salvation of sentient beings as one's own responsibility.
Why is this so? Because the path of a Bodhisattva prioritizes benefiting others; even though one has not yet attained liberation oneself, to first deliver others is the very resolve of a Bodhisattva.
Thus it is said: "I should bring all sentient beings to nirvana. This is precisely what was stated in the preceding passage: "One should give rise to such [a thought]."
"Mind. I should bring all sentient beings to nirvāṇa. To say "having brought all to nirvāṇa" means that they have been completely exhausted [in terms of delusion].
This precisely clarifies that when a bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, they must first realize that sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, being as one and not two.
Therefore, although they deliver all beings to their end, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa. As for the passage beginning with "Why is this?"...
An explanation of the inquiry: Because all sentient beings possess the mark of nirvāṇa, they cannot be further extinguished;

because all sentient beings possess the mark of bodhi, it cannot be further attained. Buddhas are precisely sentient beings who have already realized [this]; those currently in delusion are themselves Buddhas.
Therefore, within the realm of True Suchness (tathatā), the provisional names of "sentient being" and "Buddha" are cut off; within the state of equality, [there is no distinction].

There is no appearance of self or other. Although the Bodhisattva knows the equality of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and does not grasp even a single speck of dust, this does not hinder the gateway of Buddha-activities, wherein not a single dharma is abandoned.

For this reason, he performs the Buddha-activities of a phantom flower in the void, establishes a moon-in-water *maṇḍala*, subdues the demonic armies within a mirror, and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream.
For this reason, the Buddhas from time to time deliver sentient beings within their own minds, and sentient beings from time to time become the Buddhas of their own nature.
Thus, although the Buddhas deliver all sentient beings, in reality there is not a single being to be delivered;
they merely reveal what is inherently present, causing them to return to original enlightenment. This is like a physician treating the eyes: he simply removes the cataracts.
It is not that he bestows light upon them separately. Why is this? The following section investigates the meaning of delivering sentient beings while remaining free from signs.
That is to say: for what reason is it said that he brings all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, yet in reality there is not a single being who is brought to parinirvāṇa?
It is because if a bodhisattva merely conceives even a single thought of the mind to deliver others, they immediately possess the mark of a self (*ātman*). This is why...
That which is "saved" is precisely the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Not forgetting the subject and object [of the act] is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).

To be attached to this dharma is the mark of a life-span (*āyuṣka-nimitta*). If it were so, what difference would there be between such a person and an inverted ordinary worldling? Therefore, it is said that he is "not a bodhisattva.
This statement, conversely, clearly reveals that a bodhisattva who saves sentient beings must necessarily realize the non-differentiation of the three: mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.

"Separation. This refers to decisively detaching from the four marks [of self, person, being, and life]. Since one is able to detach from these marks, the method for subduing the mind does not exceed this alone.
△ Second, the explicit clarification that there is no dharma for generating the mind.
Why is this? Subhūti, there is truly no dharma whatsoever that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This passage is the direct answer that there is no such dharma for giving rise to the mind. Why is this? It is to explain the "one existence" mentioned in the preceding text.

These four characteristics we have discussed are not the true meaning of a "Bodhisattva. The intended meaning is that one is called a Bodhisattva because they are an "enlightened sentient being" (*bodhisattva*).
Thus, they seek the path of enlightenment above and transform sentient beings below;

it is by virtue of being able to give rise to the *bodhicitta* and being able to transform sentient beings that they receive this name. Nevertheless, even though this is so, one must ultimately forget this capacity.
This is what must first be attained: one must recognize the true Dharma-realm of equality. The Buddha does not deliver sentient beings;
if it were otherwise, then the four marks [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing] would remain distinct, and one would encounter obstructions at every turn.

Therefore, those who wish to give rise to the bodhicitta should know that above there is no Buddha-way to be sought, and below there are no sentient beings to be delivered. Since there is no Buddha to be sought, one does not abide [in nirvana].

The noble understanding is that there is no birth to be delivered; thus, one does not fall into the sentiments of ordinary beings. From this, the sentiments of both the noble and the ordinary are exhausted, and both person and phenomena are forgotten.
To reach this point in one's vision is called "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta); to reach this point in realization is called "attaining the fruit.

However, for a bodhisattva, at the initial moment of arousing the mind, since there is in reality no dharma that constitutes the arousal of the mind, yet there is the attainment of the fruit—[this is the true meaning].
In the state of awakening, there is likewise no dharma for the liberation of sentient beings. Therefore it is said: "In truth, there is no dharma.
Among these words, the character *wu* (無, "none" or "no") in the phrase "in truth, there is no dharma" is of the utmost importance;
it is the very core of this sutra and must not be overlooked. It is not only that there is no "existence," but furthermore, there is no "non-existence" either.
Not only is there no phenomenon (*dharma*), but there is also no non-phenomenon (*adharma*). If one looks back toward the previous stage of subduing the mind, there is no mind to be subdued;
if one dwells in the present mind, there is no mind to be dwelt upon. In the present moment, there is no *bodhi* to be realized.

Even if one looks forward to the future, there is no dharma for attaining the fruit, no dharma for receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), no dharma for turning the wheel of the Dharma, and no dharma for delivering sentient beings.

The Dharma. There is no dharma for adorning the land; there is no dharma for realizing the self. Viewing it in this way, from beginning to end, the entire text of this single fascicle of scripture finds its final resolution here:
in the single word "non-existence" (wu), everything is dissolved and brought to an end. This is what is meant by: no ordinary person and no sage; no defilement and no purity;
no high and no low; no void and no reality. Therefore, it is said: "In truth, there is nothing that can [be grasped]."
To deliver those to be delivered; to give what is given; to subdue those to be subdued;
and to dwell in that which is dwelt in—if one can truly penetrate this "dharma of no-dharma," only then is it the Bodhisattva’s arousal of the bodhicitta. Therefore, the subsequent text says:
"One who penetrates the dharma of non-self—the Tathāgata calls such a person a true Bodhisattva. This indeed possesses profound significance. As for the term "arousal" (fa):
This means "to manifest" and also "to give rise to. The character "zhě" (the one) refers to that person—namely, the one capable of giving rise to the mind.
Since the essence of this mind originally lacks even a single dharma, it is merely by practicing all wholesome dharmas through the absence of self and the absence of person that one manifests it.
This is precisely what is meant by "giving rise to [the mind] while there is no dharma; having given rise to it, there is no dharma."

Thus, we know that when a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), there is already no dharma; how much less could there be any dharma when reaching the stage of delivering sentient beings?
Alas! Had Sudhana understood this principle, why would he have traveled south to seek instruction from fifty-three masters?
[This concludes] Part Three: Showing that Cause and Effect are Without Dharma. Section One: Regarding the Fruit. Subsection One: Attaining the Fruit is Without [Dharma].
“Dharma.
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma called ‘anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’?
No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Buddha—”
"At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was no dharma by which he attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Truly, there is no dharma by which a Tathāgata attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This Buddha cites himself as witness to prove that what was previously stated is not false.
That is to say, when you heard me say that there is truly no dharma, and you resolved upon the bodhicitta—how did you understand this within the depths of your own mind?
Did you still think that there is a dharma by which one resolves upon the bodhicitta? The following interrogative passage is the World-Honored One’s use of white [speech].
This is the employment of a skillful means; it is what is called "avoiding the solid to strike the hollow" or "beating the grass to startle the snake. Why?

Because he wished to clarify the principle of the Bodhisattva’s mind being awakened through the absence of dharmas, he instead posed a question regarding his own attainment of the fruit through the absence of dharmas.

This is precisely like the *bōjiū* bird crying atop a tree while its intent lies within a field of hemp. Since he already knew that in the past, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara, [he had attained realization].

In reality, there is no dharma by which one attains the fruit. Thus, it should be known that even now, in the presence of Śākyamuni, there is likewise no dharma by which a bodhisattva generates the mind of awakening.
Therefore, it is asked: "Did the Tathāgata attain *bodhi* through any dharma at the place of Dīpaṃkara?
What is emphasized here is precisely the word "dharma. Although these words are similar to the previous inquiry regarding Dīpaṃkara, their underlying meaning is not the same.
This is redundant. That which says, "There is something attained regarding the Dharma," implies that one knows the Dharma;
this meaning belongs to another and is a perception external to the mind. This "existence of dharma" (dharmasattā) belongs to oneself and is an internal obscuration.
By interrogating with the single character "not" (a-), it is precisely intended to reveal that, in reality, there is no such dharma, thereby causing the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Unexpectedly, the one who met the occasion was truly a monk with eyes. He perfectly harmonized with the Buddha’s mind and immediately said to him, "No.

This is a case where the question is clear and the answer is direct. Nevertheless, you must recognize that within the words of this one who met the occasion there are echoes and shadows, and within his phrases there is the chronology of spring and autumn; it is not the same as the previous "No. One must distinguish between them.
This is because the intention behind the word "empty" (*śūnya*) is as follows: "To initiate" refers to the initial mind; its stage belongs to the cause.

"To attain" refers to the subsequent mind; its stage belongs to the fruit. Since there is originally no dharma that initiates the mind, how could there subsequently be any dharma that attains the fruit?
Therefore, one uses the former to explain the latter, and employs the latter to verify the former, thereby determining the meaning. Hence it is said, "No. However, according to my own understanding:
This, moreover, is the Venerable One’s phrase for shifting one's embodiment; it clearly reveals his vital, dynamic state.
The meaning is that if we discuss the Tathāgata’s present attainment of Buddhahood, which has come from the realization of Bodhi, it seems impossible to say that he does not exist.
"However, as I understand the meaning of 'the non-arising of the mind,' by this inference it would seem that one cannot attain bodhi through non-existence.
In short, I am unwilling to make a dogmatic assertion; therefore, I say, 'as I understand it.
Seeing that he was hesitating and looking about, the Tathāgata provided confirmation to settle his purpose and eliminate his uncertainty."
Therefore, it is said: "Thus. The repeated phrase "thus" is a term of affirmation, clarifying that what has been understood is correct and that there is no need for hesitation.
Why is this? Because one awakens the mind by hearing that there are no dharmas, and understands that awakening is attained through the absence of dharmas, then from beginning to end it is thus;
cause and effect are thus, without the slightest discrepancy. This is truly what is called "awakening."
In the ultimate sense, the two are not distinct. Below this, the World-Honored One feared that Subhūti might waver like a rat between two choices;
as his words remained ambiguous, he addressed him, saying: "Subhūti, you should know that when I, the Tathāgata, attained bodhi, there was truly no dharma.
This single word "truly" (實) is a definitive expression, worth more than ten thousand pieces of gold, and it is precisely this.

Mount Sumeru may be moved, but these words are difficult to alter: in reality, there is not a single dharma that exists. △ Second, the attainment of the prediction regarding the non-existence of dharmas:
"Subhūti, if there were any dharma by which the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then..."
The Buddha Dīpaṃkara did not bestow a prediction upon me, saying, "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed a prediction upon me, speaking these words:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni."
“Nī. This is a positive and negative explanation of the preceding passage, clarifying the reason for receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

However, our World-Honored One, fearing that sentient beings would be unable to develop deep faith and resolve regarding the principle of the Dharma-less, therefore reiterated the original cause through successive stages.

To demonstrate this, it is said: "If I possessed any dharma by which I attained bodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would certainly not have granted me the prediction of non-arising, saying: 'This māṇava shall become a buddha, named Śākyamuni.
One must understand that if there were a dharma by which one attains bodhi, this would be a contrary statement; it is precisely to reveal that, in reality, no such thing exists.
The Dharma; one merely attains Bodhi. The Sanskrit term *Śākya* here means "Capable One" (*Nengren*), and it is also called "Capable of Endurance" (*Nengren*).
If there were any fixed dharma-view, how could it be called "Capable of Endurance"? If one perceives signs and gives rise to the mind [of awakening], how could it be called "Capable One"?

The Sanskrit term *Muni* here means "Silent Quiescence. If dharmas truly existed, that Buddha would have transmitted them directly; why then did he record what was to come in the future? Nevertheless, he and...

"I have received [the teaching]. My three karmas are all in motion; how can this be called 'quiescence'? If there is something entrusted, there must be something bequeathed; how can this be called 'silence'?
Thus we know that the "Able One" (Śākyamuni) refers to the boundless nature of the mind, which encompasses all things.
The "Enduring One" (Kṣānti) does not perceive the arising of even the slightest dharma, nor does he perceive the cessation of even the slightest dharma. This is what is called "profound."

This is the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). As for "silent stillness," it is stillness that is ever-illuminating, and illumination that is ever-still;
stillness and illumination are mutually fused. Thus, when speaking, one is silent; when silent, one speaks. Therefore, though speaking, there is no speaking; though silent, it is not silence.
Until the paths of mental activity are cut off and the ways of language are severed, one wondrously enters the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and profoundly penetrates [reality].
It is only when one realizes the principle that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma that one attains this prediction and receives this auspicious title; truly, it is as the saying goes:
"there is no emptiness beneath a name. For this reason, one knows that Bodhi does not exist subsequent to the arousal of the mind, nor is it attained subsequent to liberation.
If even the fruit of Buddhahood is thus, so too is the causal mind. Thus, in reality, there is nothing [to be gained].
The meaning of "the existence of dharmas" can now be clarified. It is said that although gold dust is precious, it becomes mere grime when it falls into the eye.

Were there even a single dharma, it would not be the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*), nor the fundamental reality of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). △ Third, the turning explanation of the non-existence of dharmas, in two parts:
first, the explanation of the existence of dharmas; second, the correct explanation of the non-existence of dharmas. First, the correct explanation of the non-existence of dharmas.
Why is this? "Tathāgata" has the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This passage further explains the reason why one attains the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that "no dharma exists. The section beginning with "Why is this so?
provides the interrogation and the explanation. That is to say: for what reason must there truly be no dharma before one can receive the prediction?
Indeed, when Dīpaṃkara predicted my name as "Buddha," it was the ninth title of the Dharmakāya; when he predicted my name as "Tathāgata," it was the [tenth] title of the Dharmakāya.
"Number one. However, apart from the Dharmakāya, there is no separate dharma that can be called the Tathāgata. To say "Tathāgata" is precisely the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
This is truly the old fellow calling his own bluff and explaining it himself; it is what they mean by "a father does not notice the ugliness of his son.
The meaning of the suchness of all dharmas refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth—all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharmas.
This is the meaning of *tathatā* (Suchness). The Buddha realized this principle and is therefore called the *Tathāgata*. However, this single name applies to both ordinary beings and sages;
it is only because sentient beings are shrouded by the false imaginings and attachments of their deluded minds that they are termed *tathā-gata* ("thus gone").

One must understand that although they have "gone," they have not actually departed. The Buddhas, through the wisdom of non-abiding and detachment from all signs, have thoroughly realized *tathatā* and are thus named [the Tathāgatas].
The Tathāgata should be known as coming while there is no coming; thus one knows that he is as originally uncoming, for his coming is from suchness.
This precisely means that when a pond is dug, the moon is not created; yet once the pond is formed, the moon comes of its own accord. It is truly because of all sentient beings [that this occurs].
To come while not being as [the Tathāgata] is the small sage who has transcended the world (*lokottara*). To be as [the Tathāgata] yet not to come is the Bodhisattva of provisional rank;

though they are as [the Tathāgata], they have not yet fully realized "as-ness," and even if they were to come, they could not yet fully manifest "coming. Only Buddha-to-Buddha can fully realize "as-ness" and fully manifest "coming.
To fully realize "as-ness" is to exhaust the limit of True Suchness (*tathatā*); to fully manifest "coming" is to empty the realm of sentient beings. By means of this...
For this reason, one is called a Tathāgata. This [name] comes from true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);

it is the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*) regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*). Regarding the passage beginning with "If there is someone who says," it means that there are people in the world who do not understand that the name "Tathāgata" is the meaning of true suchness within all phenomena, but instead imagine that there is a separate dharma which, upon attaining bodhi, is first named [Tathāgata].
"Tathāgata. If one errs by even a hair's breadth, one misses the mark by a thousand li; such a person does not understand the meaning of "Tathāgata.
This is because the Tathāgata comes from the sense of the "suchness" (tathatā) of all dharmas.

Thus, at all times and in all places, there is nothing that is not "such," and nothing that is not "coming. What is called "such" does not abide in suchness; there is nowhere it goes that is not such.
Coming, there is no coming; not coming, yet there is no non-coming. Thus, in every matter all is as it is, and in every dharma all is fully present.
How, then, could Dīpaṃkara Buddha have had any dharma to give? And how could I have had any dharma to receive?
Therefore it is said: "Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi. What is emphasized here lies precisely in the word "attain" (得).
That which is called "unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment" is simply another name for *tathatā* (suchness).
This is inherently possessed by every person; were one to realize this equal suchness, then all things and phenomena would be without deficiency.
There is nothing remaining; there is no deficiency; there is nothing to be added. Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed.

Comprehending this principle, one practices through illusion on the ground and realizes through illusion within the fruit. Every single thing is the whole, and every object is fully manifest. This is termed "Perfect Equality."

If one can truly awaken to Suchness (*tathatā*), suddenly emptying the four marks and thoroughly realizing the three voids—like a lotus flower blooming or awakening from a dream—one is called "Perfectly Awakened" (*samyaksambuddha*).
There is no such thing as this Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Perfect Awakening to be attained apart from Suchness.
Therefore, the Buddha decisively declared: "In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains Bodhi. △
Second, the explanation of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma:
Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi contains neither reality nor unreality.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti, as for what is said...
"All dharmas" are precisely not all dharmas; therefore they are called "all dharmas.
This pair of explanations—using "neither real nor unreal"—clarifies how one receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) within the context of the "unrecorded" (*avyākṛta*).
By stating that "all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma," it explains the meaning of "the suchness of all dharmas. Thus, Subhūti said...
"Ti. The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata is the principle of the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
Within this, there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous; it is what is called that which does not increase when in the state of a sage, nor decrease when among ordinary people.
It is the equality of True Suchness (tathatā), the wondrous Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). It cannot be seen through physical forms."
Because it is sought through verbal expression, it is said to be "without reality. This is why the preceding passage states that "there is truly no dharma":

this refers to the fact that no dharma can be apprehended as a recordable entity. Nevertheless, it is not apart from the external characteristics of form; there is no separate, equal *tathatā* (suchness) existing elsewhere.
Nor is there, apart from language, a separate, ultimate principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is said to be "not false. This refers to the preceding passage...
Therefore it is said: "For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me a prediction, saying: 'In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Śākyamuni. This refers to the fact that one receives a prediction by means of the non-existence of dharmas.

Thus, the two characters 'for this' (is-hu) refer back to what the Tathāgata previously stated regarding 'all dharmas,' namely the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), elements (dhātus), and so forth, which belong to the world."
The teaching that "all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma" means that they are precisely the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
This is the correct explanation of "Tathāgata," which refers to the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:

"These five aggregates, six sense bases, from the twelve bases up to the eighteen elements, are all the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of true suchness. This follows the passage spoken by Subhūti below.
This establishes the meaning of being neither substantial nor void. For it is said that all dharmas are none other than the one mind;
the mind is itself the dharma, and the dharma is itself the mind. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks in accordance with this nature:

the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests, the straightness of pines and the curvature of thorns, the whiteness of cranes and the blackness of crows—all of these...

Within the mind of *tathatā* (suchness), there is the Buddha-dharma of intrinsic nature. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Livelihood, occupations, and so forth—all are in accord with the True Dharma.
This means that the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature, and the illusory, empty body is itself the *dharmakāya*.
Consequently, there is not a single dharma that is not *tathatā*. This is precisely what is meant by the statement that worldly conventional expressions all accord with the Way. Who...?
The strings and pipes of the home do not transmit the mind; therefore, the Buddha spoke of all phenomena (dharmas) according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
As for the phrase "it is not," this means that one must not cling to the notion that all phenomena are themselves the true nature of reality (tathatā) or the Buddha-dharma.
If you claim that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, then point them out one by one right here before us: among all these phenomena, which one is the Buddha?

That is suchness (*tathatā*). Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is empty and quiescent, and because from the beginning there have been no worlds or sentient beings, it is said that they "are not all phenomena.
This is what the Buddha spoke in reliance upon ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, [the passage] correctly clarifies that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma—namely, those that are defiled or pure, noble or ordinary, and those with conceptual attachment or without.
Sentient beings, all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds—there is not one that is not the Buddha-dharma.
It is precisely these lush green bamboo, the dense yellow flowers, the lofty mountains, and the flowing waters; there is not a single dharma that is not True Suchness (Tathatā) and the Buddha-dharma.
This is taught in reliance upon the Middle Way of the Supreme Truth (Paramārtha-satya), which is simultaneously the conventional and the ultimate. Indeed.
To know that all is not all is to be without reality; to know that all is indeed all is clearly to be without falsehood.
It is also said that at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the Buddha had no dharma to attain; therefore, it is called "without reality.
Because there was nothing to be attained, he was able to become a Buddha today, named Śākyamuni. This is why it is so.
It is not false. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy:

"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was tall and large. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person whose body is tall and large, that is precisely what is called 'not a large body'; it is designated as a 'large body' [only figuratively]."

This uses a metaphor to conclude the teaching. In the preceding text, the great body of Mount Sumeru was used as a metaphor for the fact that although there is nothing upon which to dwell, one should nevertheless give rise to the bodhicitta.
Here, again, the "non-body" and "great body" serve as metaphors for the principle that while all dharmas are not [ultimately] existent, they are nonetheless called "all dharmas.
This establishes that because there is truly no dharma, one should resolve to attain bodhicitta. Thus, the Buddha said, for example:
The "greatness of the human body" corresponds to what was stated in the preceding text: that all dharmas are metaphorical for the *dharmakāya* of true thusness (*tathatā*).

Being omnipresent within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and possessing immeasurable merits, it is called "great"; this refers to the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*). Subhūti said, "World-Honored One..."

The Tathāgata says that the human body is large; this "large body" is precisely not a large body. This corresponds to the preceding text which states "not all dharmas," serving as a metaphor for the *tathatā-dharmakāya*.
Being free from all hindrances and abiding alone in ultimate truth, it is called "large"; this constitutes its "great function. Thus it is named the "large body.
This corresponds to the preceding text which states "this is named all dharmas," serving as a metaphor for the *tathatā-dharmakāya*. That is to say:
The conventional is itself the ultimate; possessing both characteristics and function, it is called the "wondrously great. This is the "greatness of essence" (*tattva-mahat*).

Therefore, the Treatise says: "That which is not a body has no characteristics; that which is called the 'Great Body' possesses the essence of *tathatā*, and is thus named the 'Wondrously Great Body.'"
Question: The sutra text merely introduces the analogy, "It is like a person’s body being large and tall. The Buddha’s discourse seems not yet finished;

how could the one who is responsive to the teaching (the *dharmabhāṇaka*) suddenly interject in mid-air, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large and tall, it is precisely a non-large body;
it is called a 'large body'"? If this were so, would the one responsive to the teaching not be acting with reckless superficiality? Answer: Examine the remainder [of the text].

This pattern appears consistently across the five translations. Upon careful examination of its underlying intent, one realizes that these are not the words of the Buddha’s response to the specific occasion (*pratyarha*).
Rather, they are the concluding testimony for this section, referring back to the passage already understood by the interlocutor within the preceding chapter on "Non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*).
As it says: "When I speak of all dharmas, they are not all dharmas; they are called 'all dharmas'. This serves to clarify the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
As with the Dharma-body, it is not "great" that makes it great. I have previously told you, for example, that a human body is large and tall.
You, Subhūti, said: "What the Tathāgata calls a 'large and tall human body' is itself not a large body; it is merely named a 'large body.'"
Since you already know that the absence of abiding previously was considered great, you should likewise know that this non-existence of dharmas is also great. Why do you still harbor further doubts?

This precisely illustrates that when the fruit is formed, there are no dharmas present. II. Regarding the cause, there are three parts. First, clarifying that there are no dharmas for saving sentient beings.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva. If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," that person would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that is called a "bodhisattva.
Therefore, among all dharmas, the Buddha taught that there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
This demonstrates that there is, in reality, no dharma called "Bodhisattva"; one should, prior to this, give rise to such a mind.
This is because, as the Tathāgata previously cited his own experience at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was truly no dharma by which he generated the bodhicitta.
This is established as a standard for Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is specifically shown here: "A Bodhisattva is also like this.
If they were to give rise to even a single thought, 'I can deliver sentient beings,' they would not be a Bodhisattva. Why?

Because if there are sentient beings to be delivered, then subject and object are not forgotten, and the four marks remain distinct. How, then, could they be called a Bodhisattva? Therefore, it is said: 'That is not a Bodhisattva.'"
“Sā. “Then how, pray tell, does one become a bodhisattva? “Listen, Subhūti, you should understand this:

if one speaks according to reality, one must shatter the three attachments, realize the three emptinesses, and comprehend that all phenomena are like illusions—the wondrous essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*), which is entirely one and equal. Apart from this, there is truly no other dharma; only then can one be so named.”
In his capacity as a bodhisattva, for this reason, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are indeed the Buddha-dharma;
thus, there are no longer the four marks. Therefore, it is said: "For this reason, all dharmas are devoid of the marks of self, person, and so forth.
Because the self, person, and so forth do not exist, both subject and object are empty, and even that emptiness itself is empty.
In reality, not a single dharma corresponds to the mind. Thus, although the Bodhisattva spends his entire day saving beings, there is not a single being who can be saved;
although he speaks all day long, there is not a single dharma that can be spoken.
This is precisely what is meant by the Bodhisattva’s “saving without saving” and “not saving while saving. △ Second, clarifying that there are no dharmas for adorning the land.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls adorning the buddha-fields is itself not adorning; it is merely designated as "adorning."
This demonstrates the self-nature of *tathatā*. In the stage of the *dharmakāya*, there is likewise no land to be adorned; therefore, it is said:

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva who seeks what is above and transforms those below should give rise to even a single thought of subject and object—thinking 'I can adorn the Buddha-land'—this is to boast of one's own virtue and to claim credit for one's own achievements.
It is precisely this that constitutes the failure to extinguish the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*)."
Since all four characteristics are fully present, how could one be called a Bodhisattva who seeks supreme enlightenment above and transforms sentient beings below?
Therefore, it is said that he is "not a Bodhisattva. Why is this so? To explain the inquiry: because it is the self-nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
The Bodhi-Dharmakāya cannot be adorned by words. Why is this so?
It is because the Tathāgata has always taught Bodhisattvas to cultivate the six pāramitās in order to transform sentient beings and adorn Buddha-lands.

That which was previously taught regarding adornment was explained according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) to clarify that the True Suchness Dharmakāya possesses adornment. Today, however, [the teaching] is...
That which is not adorned refers to the Dharmakāya of True Suchness as spoken of from the perspective of ultimate truth.
It is primordially pure, like the great void. To desire to adorn it would be like boring holes into primordial chaos or painting eyebrows upon empty space;
it may be called creating trouble where there was none. One must know that when the mind is pure, the land is pure—what need is there for further adornment? Therefore...

"To say 'adornment' is itself non-adornment" clarifies that the essence of the thing is entirely empty. "This is called [adornment]" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), clarifying that the *dharmakāya* of True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not fall into existence or non-existence and is far removed from ordinary beings and sages.
Although there is no adornment, one does not discard adornment; therefore, it is said, "this is called adornment. This is adornment within non-adornment.

In this [section], he speaks of adornment. He correctly instructs bodhisattvas to purify buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity by means of the playful exercise of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
△ Third, he clearly understands that there is no self and no dharmas.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata declares him to be a true bodhisattva;

this concludes that, in reality, there is no such thing as a bodhisattva-dharma. This precisely refers to the adornment of saving sentient beings. Thus it is through successive investigation and inquiry.
In truth, there is no such dharma. Nevertheless, Subhūti, why is it that anyone who speaks of there being beings to be delivered or lands to be adorned is not called a bodhisattva?
It is because only one who can penetrate the dharma of non-self is a bodhisattva.
If one says there are beings who can be delivered, then they have not realized that the nature of sentient beings is empty. If one says there are lands that can be...
Yan: This is because one has not realized that the nature of all phenomena is empty. Thus, while the three attachments are fully present, the three emptinesses remain hidden.

How, then, could such a person be called a Bodhisattva? Therefore, it is said that they do not even bear that name. Now, since one has thoroughly realized here that the nature of sentient beings is empty, one naturally lacks attachment to a self;
and since one has realized that the nature of all phenomena is empty, one naturally lacks attachment to either phenomena or non-phenomena. These three—

By grasping and shattering [these views], the three emptinesses are revealed; therefore, the Tathāgata says that such a person is truly a bodhisattva. Regarding the scriptural passage here, it should state:
"Thoroughly penetrating non-self and non-dharmas"—only then would its meaning be complete. This is because the Qin translation is still deficient, lacking the single character "non" (wu).
Furthermore, there are three instances in the scripture where the phrase "is not a bodhisattva" occurs; the first refers to the one who can generate the mind [of awakening].

Next, [the text] refers to those who can deliver sentient beings; third, it refers to the lands they adorn. In all these cases, it uses reductio ad absurdum to show that if one does not realize the emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), one is not a bodhisattva.
At this point, the meaning of the text reaches its ultimate conclusion; therefore, it concludes accordingly by stating:

"If one is truly a bodhisattva, one must necessarily realize the emptiness of both person and phenomena; only then is one called 'truly' [a bodhisattva]. Furthermore, the two characters "truly" (*zhen shi*) invert the preceding [negation].
"It is not so. This is the wondrous resonance of the Buddha’s words—like a pearl rolling upon a tray, or a lion casting its cub;
not a single point is left empty. To say "truly a Bodhisattva" means one is able to penetrate this Dharma. What is called "penetration" (tōng) means there is nothing that can obstruct;
what is called "mastery" (dá) means there is no dharma that can hinder. This is precisely the single aperture through which all is void and penetrating, opening in all eight directions.
Linglong! Formless and selfless, spring enters its proper order; unretaining and unobstructed, the moon travels through space.

If it is thus, only then is one a thorough master of non-self and dharmas. One does not enter into the deluded sentiments of the mundane world, nor does one fall into the saintly understandings of the supramundane.
This is one who has truly generated the bodhicitta and is a true Bodhisattva. Should one fail to realize this, one cannot be called a Bodhisattva.
△ Second, directly revealing the essential body of Prajñā; this has two parts. First, a careful demonstration; this has three parts.
First, regarding the three aspects of the perfection and clarity of knowledge and vision: first, to demonstrate the Buddha’s vision and perfect vision.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "So it is, World-Honored One."
He possesses the divine eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom eye? "It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma eye? "It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma eye. Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha eye?
"No. It is so, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.
This is because the preceding text stated that one who penetrates the truth of non-self and non-dharmas is truly a bodhisattva.

Fearing that such a bodhisattva might not yet recognize the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā) being unchanging while skillfully conforming to conditions, they might instead cling to it as mere 'non-self.'"

There is no way [to attain it]. This alone is the true Bodhisattva. One might think that although the two attachments to the dharmas of arising and non-arising must ultimately be known to be absent, if one were to fixate on this as being definitively correct, one would again be sitting within the state of dual emptiness (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*).
This is precisely what Yunmen meant when he said that the Dharma-body has two kinds of illnesses.

When one reaches the realm of the Dharma-body, because the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) has not been forgotten and one's own views still persist, this is the first illness. Even if one manages to penetrate the Dharma-body, it must not be let go of;
if one carefully examines it, what trace remains? That too is an illness. Thus, Mañjuśrī for a moment...
The arising of the view of dharmas is precisely this: [the claim] that the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power encompasses and enters within the two Iron Ring Mountains.
This is because one knows only that which is quiescent and unmoving as being the ultimate realization; thus, one fails to understand the principle of "responding and penetrating without being moved.
Is this not to be drowned to death in stagnant water? Therefore, the Buddha questioned him point by point in order to bring it forth and clarify it.
Indeed, it is because the Tathāgata is perfectly endowed with the five eyes that he is able to penetrate and see the three minds. Since the mind is no-mind, the nature of sentient beings is empty.
Having realized this principle, although he spends his days delivering sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings to be delivered.
This teaching shows that although Bodhisattvas lack a self or dharmas, they do not hinder the arising of function in accordance with their nature, which blazes forth.

Nevertheless, in order to deliver sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s five eyes are taught; these do not depart from the flesh-eyes of sentient beings, thereby clearly manifesting the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas.
This serves to corroborate the preceding passage. Therefore, this is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s statement that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Here, he first asks: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess flesh-eyes?"
"No. Now tell me, for what reason did the old man Gautama pose this question?

The underlying intent of this opportune response is that even if one were to gaze upon the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are still located on the Buddha's face; thus it is said, "The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
What does this mean? How could the Great Teacher of the Three Realms and Compassionate Father of the Four Births not [possess such vision]?
To know whether one possesses the eye or lacks it in ordinary times, one must turn toward the lips of the person facing the situation to seek news and investigate the ultimate point.
This is because our World-Honored One truly had a profound intention; thus he asked, "Does the Tathāgata still possess the fleshly eye?
With this single question, he placed the very essence of Prajñā and the impartial True Suchness upon the table, offering it all at once.
It emerges. Why? Because in responding to the capacity of the occasion, it is said that there is the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).

Since the fleshly eye exists, our Tathāgata is no different from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, since ordinary beings also possess the fleshly eye, how could ordinary beings ever not be Buddhas?
Therefore, the statement that "there is the fleshly eye" clarifies the path of the equality of birth and Buddhahood. Again, he asked: "The Tathāgata possesses the divine [eye]..."

"No, [he does not have] the eye. This response was intended to address the immediate concern: since the Buddha is titled "God among Gods" (*devātideva*), how could he not possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)?

Thus, it is said that he possesses the divine eye; if so, how would our Tathāgata differ from the various devas? Furthermore, since the devas also possess the divine eye, how would they differ from the Buddha?
This clarifies that devas and Buddhas are equal. Next, he asked again: "Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*)?"
This "eye of wisdom" (prajñā-cakṣus) is that which is possessed by the noble ones (ārya) of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The eye of wisdom I have attained since ancient times is this very one. However, the interlocutor, considering the Buddha to be the most holy among the holy, asks how he could possibly lack the eye of wisdom;
thus, [the Buddha] replies: "I possess the eye of wisdom. Since I possess the eye of wisdom, how am I, the Tathāgata, any different from the lesser sages? Nevertheless...
Furthermore, since the Lesser Sage (Śrāvaka) also possesses the eye of wisdom, how does he differ from the Buddha?
This precisely demonstrates the equality of the Lesser and the Great Vehicles. Yet [the text] further asks: "Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?

The intention of the interlocutor is that since the Buddha is titled the King of the Dharma, how could he not possess the Dharma-eye? Thus it is said that he possesses the Dharma-eye. Since he possesses the Dharma-eye, then I—
"In that case, how does the Tathāgata differ from a bodhisattva? If so, the bodhisattva also possesses the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, what distinction is there between a bodhisattva and a Buddha? This clarifies the equality of cause and effect. When the Tathāgata reached this point, he asked again:
"Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye? The one present [Mañjuśrī] replied: "One who has perfected the three types of awakening is called a Buddha; how could he lack the Buddha-eye?"
Because of the Buddha-eye, he answered: "There is the Buddha-eye. Since there is the Buddha-eye, I, the Tathāgata, am no different from all Buddhas;
furthermore, all Buddhas also possess the Buddha-eye, which is not distinct from me, the Tathāgata.

This reveals that only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; it is the sameness of the Way among all Buddhas. It is not only [the case for] Buddhas and...
All Buddhas are identical. Furthermore, when among ordinary beings they are the same as ordinary beings; when among devas they are the same as devas; when among sages they are the same as sages;

when among bodhisattvas they are the same as bodhisattvas; and when among Buddhas they are the same as Buddhas. This is what is meant by: "Though the streams and mountains differ, the wind and moon are the same.

This clearly elucidates the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*), the fundamental essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). It does not increase when in the state of a sage, nor does it decrease when among ordinary beings.
[The previous category] is diminished. Therefore, when the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, this is what he means.

However, if one discusses the aforementioned five eyes from a restricted perspective, each has its own distinct characteristics: the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is unobstructed, while the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is obstructed and lacks such penetration;

the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) observes only the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), while the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) perceives true emptiness (*bhūtashūnyatā*); and the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) is like a thousand suns.

Illuminating their distinct natures, they are seen to be ultimately identical. By this principle, each subsequent stage is superior to the preceding one, while each preceding stage is inferior to the subsequent one.
Thus, ordinary beings possess only one; devas and humans possess two; the lesser sages possess three; bodhisattvas possess four;

and only Buddhas possess all five. Therefore, they penetrate and perceive True Suchness (Tathatā), wherein the conceptualizations of "sentient being" and "Buddha" are empty, and all is equal in the single mark.
...Indeed. △ Second, showing the Buddha’s perfect knowledge.
Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding all the sands in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say they are sand?
"Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata says they are sand. Subhūti, what do you think? As for a single Ganges River...
"Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in all those rivers.
Would the number of Buddha-worlds equal to the number of grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers be many? "Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has taught that..."
The mind is entirely non-mind; this is what is called "mind. Why is that? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended;
the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
The above clarifies the Buddha’s eye of vision; this clarifies the arising of the mind that perceives. Subhūti, what do you think?
Is it not the case that when the Buddha speaks of the sands of the Ganges River, he says they are sand? This is a verification based on actual facts.
From the words "In this way, World-Honored One" onwards, the disciple immediately attests to his faith. The Buddha possesses the fleshly eye (māṃsa-cakṣus), no different [from others].
Ordinary worldlings, when they say this is sand, the Buddha also says it is sand. However, ordinary worldlings only know that it is sand;
they do not know how many grains there are in a single river’s sand. The Buddha knows this. This is the fleshly eye possessed by the Buddha;
although he manifests as being the same as ordinary worldlings, he is beyond their reach. Subhūti, regarding this—
The meaning of the passage beginning with "What do you think? is as follows: [The Buddha] said that the number of grains of sand in a single Ganges River is equal to the number of worlds.
This serves as proof that the Buddha possesses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). A single Ganges River is forty *li* in length, and the sand within it is as fine as flour.

If one were to take a single grain of sand and divert a river for each grain until all the sand was exhausted, the number of Ganges Rivers would be immeasurable. By diverting such infinite Ganges Rivers...

Regarding worlds: suppose there is one grain of sand; let us calculate one world for each grain. Since each world consists of a trichiliocosm (a system of three thousand great thousand worlds), worlds would thus become immeasurable and boundless.
Even if the gods among the heavens were able to know as many worlds as the sands of a single river, that would suffice;
how much more so when the sands equal the Ganges River itself, and those sands are further divided into worlds, with each world likewise [expanding].
Each possesses the numerical extent of a trichiliocosm, such that even the eyes of the various devas cannot reach them.
Yet, although the Buddha speaks of the "divine eye," he is able to see them all completely; this is precisely what is meant by the saying:

"Mountains and rivers are within the divine eye; the world is within the Dharma-body. Although the Buddha manifests as having the divine eye, it is something that the various devas cannot attain. Thus, the Buddha declared:
From "Subhūti" onwards, it clarifies the reality of the Buddha’s possession of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). As for the term "land," it refers to the world-systems;

that is, world-systems as numerous as the sands of immeasurable and boundless oceans. Within each world-system, there are a certain number of sentient beings, and each sentient being possesses a certain nature of mind.
Even if one possessed the wisdom-eye of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), even if they had the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), they would still not [be able to know them].
And so it is here. Although the Buddha manifests a wisdom-eye identical [to that of others], he perceives everything without distinguishing between the sentient beings and their environment;
this is why he transcends the two vehicles, and the wisdom-eye of the two vehicles cannot be compared to his. Why is this?

The following section interrogates and clarifies the reality of the Buddha’s possession of the Dharma-eye, asking: for what reason does he perceive the minds of living beings throughout the sands of the Ganges?
The Buddha knows them all completely. *Nian*. Although the mental activities of sentient beings are numerous, they do not exceed the deluded consciousness of perversion as their mind;
none of these are the true, eternally abiding mind. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all minds are "not-mind.
That which is called "mind" is precisely a statement that deluded consciousness originally has no substantial reality, possessing nothing more than the mere name "mind."
That is all. Although a Bodhisattva possesses the Dharma-eye, they have not yet fully seen that the arising of the mind is entirely illusory and that all phenomena are utterly empty.
However, although a Buddha is called the Dharma-eye, he is able to know and see everything completely; thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"I am the all-knowing one and the all-seeing one. Even you, gods and humans, should all come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Viewed in this light, the Dharma-eye of a Bodhisattva is, moreover, beyond reach. Why is this?
[The following] interrogates and explains how that which is not mind is taken as mind, thereby proving that the Buddha is endowed with the Buddha-eye."
"True. This means that although such sand-grained worlds are boundless and sentient beings are immeasurable, with their various mental natures, the Buddha knows them all.
Why is this? It is because all sentient beings undergo the flux of the three periods of time;
their deluded minds originally possess no substantial reality and are entirely ungraspable. Therefore, it is said that the past, present, and future are all ungraspable.
It is attained. This is because it is said that the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide.
An ancient master once said: "When one seeks the mind throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not to be found. Where the mind is not to be found, delusive conditions are absent.

Where delusive conditions are absent, that is *bodhi*. Birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally equal. One should know that the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) is the most supreme among the five eyes.
Seeking its ultimate limit, one does not find it outside of the point where the mind of the three periods of time cannot be apprehended;

this is why the previous chapter repeatedly instructed the Bodhisattva to resolve his mind to save sentient beings and adorn the Buddha-land—all of which are unapprehendable, for there is truly no dharma that constitutes "mind.
This is precisely what Chan Master Xuefeng sought when he asked Dharma Master Bodhidharma for peace of mind, to which the Master replied:
"Bring forth your mind so that I may settle it for you. [The Master] replied, "When I seek my mind, it is utterly unattainable.
Mazu said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. Thereupon, Deshan went to a woman to buy oil-cakes as a snack.
The woman asked, "The three minds are unattainable; which one of the minds will you eat? Deshan had no reply. It was only upon reaching Longtan that he finally blew out the paper lamp.
[The Master] said, "Even so, you will only have attained the manifestation of a 'mind that cannot be grasped. Now, tell me, everyone:
what exactly is this 'mind that cannot be grasped'? Do not, by any means, understand it as 'three pounds of flax' or a 'dry dung pellet'!"
If one has such a view, one has already fallen into the "attainable mind. Even if one does not have such a view, one still falls into the "attainable mind.
△ Third, showing that true merit is not [ordinary] merit, in two parts. First, clarifying that while there is reality, it is not much.

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? "So it is, World-Honored One;
that person would acquire very great merit by reason of this."
This refers back to the preceding text, which stated that the three minds cannot be apprehended. Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose there were a person who, taking the non-apprehendable mind as the cause and using the filling of a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures as the condition, gave them as a gift to others. Would this person, by reason of these causes and conditions, acquire much merit?

The interlocutor says, “So it is, World-Honored One. Regarding this phrase “so it is,” it correctly clarifies that by means of the mind of non-apprehension, one accords with suchness—that is, the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, one should respond in unison with the voice [of the Buddha], saying, “So it is, World-Honored One.
Since this person has taken the mind of non-apprehension as the cause and the giving of the seven treasures as the condition, and furthermore—
To practice the giving of the seven treasures while further not dwelling upon signs results in merit that evokes the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); it is truly immense.
Regarding this term "immense": even if one gives the seven treasures while dwelling upon signs, the merit is already vast;
how much more so when one does not dwell upon signs—how could the resulting merit and virtue not be immensely great? In other translations, following the phrase "immense," all [versions]...
There is a Buddha who says, "It is so, it is so. The Qin translation omits this. Someone may ask:
"If the mind is ultimately unattainable, then the cultivation of merit is likewise unattainable. How, then, can one obtain such vast merit? How is this to be reconciled? Answer:
Have you not heard? The rhinoceros develops patterns on its horn because it gazes at the moon; the elephant has flowers appear in its tusks because it was startled by thunder.

Indeed, the moon has no intention toward the rhinoceros, yet as the rhinoceros gazes upon it, the patterns arise; the thunder has no conscious intent toward the elephant, yet as the elephant is startled by it, the flowers emerge.
By analogy with these cases, it is the same for the thunder that causes the plantain tree to grow, or the iron that turns toward the magnet—all function through such natural resonance.
There is no mind, yet there is this power. If even material things are thus, how could it not be so according to principle?
Thus we know that the "unobtainable mind" is the attainment of non-attainment; this is indeed the Great Attainment. Therefore, though the words are many, what is there left to doubt?
△ Second, clarifying that because it lacks substantial reality, it is "much.
Subhūti, if merit possessed substantial reality, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains much merit.
Because merit lacks substantial reality, the Tathāgata says that one obtains much merit.

In this instance, the Tathāgata answers according to the capacity of the listener regarding the abundance of merit. He turns the discourse with a sudden shift in phrasing, causing him to ascend the hall and enter the chamber.
Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one obtains "abundant merit.
This precisely clarifies the gift of the jewels of the great trichiliocosm. If there were an emergence of a [substantial] mind, it would all be defiled conduct; yet the merit obtained...
[This is] limited and moreover not real. The Tathāgata would certainly not have said that one gains much merit.
By the above, it is shown by contrast that because the mind is not real, the merit is also not much.
Since merit does not exist, when the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit, this is an affirmative explanation. As for what is called "much," it is because one acts with this ungraspable mind.

Regarding the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*): one deeply penetrates that merit is by nature fundamentally empty and devoid of any expectation. One must understand that although one does not anticipate merit, merit is spontaneously accomplished.
This is just like clouds and wind in an empty valley; yet the valley does not expect the wind and clouds, and they arrive of their own accord.
It is also like the grasses and trees in the deep mountains; the mountain does not make an appointment with the grasses and trees, yet they flourish naturally.

Then the grasses and trees will grow of themselves. Thus we know that when one practices giving with a mind of non-attainment and abides in the non-abiding, the merit obtained is the fruit of the untainted, unconditioned, and unsurpassed;
therefore it is said to be "very much. In this context, the word "non-" (wu) [refers to the absence of conceptual grasping].
This is precisely the "non-existence" that is free from characteristics and non-abiding; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is vast.
However, this passage correctly clarifies that the Buddha possesses the five eyes and perceives the three minds through to their depths.

He fully knows and fully sees the two types of practice—phenomenal and principled—and the varying degrees of merit of all sentient beings. This serves to reveal the equal fundamental essence, which cannot be sought through a mind possessed of intentional thought.
Furthermore, one must not seek by means of a state of no-mind; rather, it is taught that for us, when not a single thought arises, the entire body [of reality] manifests.
This is what is meant by "attaining thus within that which cannot be attained. △ Second, the three points concerning form, characteristics, and verbal expression.
First, it shows that form is non-form.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body endowed with physical form? "No, World-Honored One."

One should not see the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the physical body. Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the perfection of the physical body is itself not the perfection of the physical body;
it is merely designated as the "perfection of the physical body."
This explains the preceding passage. If merit were substantial, it would not be called "much"; it is because merit is insubstantial that the Tathāgata speaks of it as "much.
Regarding the section beginning with "Subhūti, what do you think?"—it means that among all worldly and world-transcending merits, none exceed those of the Buddha;
namely, his adornment of myriad virtues and his marks and signs of a hundred blessings, which may indeed be called "much."
Therefore, he raised the matter of perceiving the physical body (*rūpakāya*) in order to examine it closely, wishing to let those present realize that this merit is substantial;
thus, he did not speak of its being "much. Hence he asked, "Can one perceive the physical body as complete?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. This single response alone conveys the meaning that this merit is substantial and not merely "much."
Thus, it is self-evident without the need for further debate. Therefore, it is resolved: "The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the body of perfected form.
This precisely reveals that the Buddha is not to be seen as form; for the pure Dharma-body is like empty space.

Manifesting forms in accordance with sentient beings, like the moon reflected in water—how could one perceive this through physical form? This precisely reveals that merit and virtue have no substantial reality;
it is for this reason that the Tathāgata speaks of "much. As for the term "endowed," it refers to the accomplishment of the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*).

Regarding these eighty types, their names are recorded in the numerical categories of the Dharma; they shall not be described here at length. Those who require them should consult [the relevant texts].
This clarifies that there is no excellence not possessed and no mark lacking. As for what is called the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*), it refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) of the Tathāgata.
Although it lacks marks and lacks excellence, it nonetheless does not transcend the category of form-dharmas;
therefore, it is called the "form-body. Viewed in this light, even the Tathāgata’s complete form-body still belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If even a single speck of dust cannot defile the fundamental substance of prajñā, how much less so can the physical bodies of the three vehicles or the six realms?
One should know that once one falls into a physical body, it immediately belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is not the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fundamental substance.

Therefore, the following provides an evidentiary explanation: When the Tathāgata habitually speaks of the physical body (rūpakāya) adorned with the myriad virtues and the marks and signs of a hundred merits, for what reason is this?
It is because the Buddha, in accordance with conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), speaks of the fulfillment of the physical body; yet, in accordance with ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)...
To say that it is "not a complete physical body" accords with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Middle Way;

to say that "this is called a complete physical body" is what is meant here by stating that one should not view it as being complete—this is spoken from the perspective of the absolute truth (*tattva*).
△ Second, showing that the marks themselves are free from marks.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks? No, World-Honored One;

The marks are likewise all the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma-body. Are they not, indeed, the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the very essence of Prajñā?
△ Third, showing that speaking is non-speaking.

For this reason, I have cautioned you, Subhūti: do not entertain such thoughts. However, in...

This is called a "Dharma-preacher. It means that the Tathāgata is both the conventional and the ultimate, both emptiness and existence;

This is precisely what is meant by the statement that during his forty-nine years, he never uttered a single word. △ Third, regarding sentient beings:

The Buddha said, “Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings. Why is this?

"Sentient beings are not non-sentient beings. Why is this so? Subhūti, one must understand that the repetition of the term "sentient beings" is intended to explain the meaning of the preceding two phrases; it means that they are indeed not [ultimately] sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*): what is its intended meaning? The following two phrases provide the direct explanation.

That is to say, when the Tathāgata speaks of "non-sentient beings," he means that they are not ordinary, mundane sentient beings; when he says "these are called sentient beings," he is speaking of sentient beings who possess the nature of the sages (*ārya*).
Now, although sages are also termed "sentient beings," this is merely a name; in reality, they are not ordinary beings.

Regarding these sentient beings: if one explains them by way of the three truths, the fact that these sentient beings who possess faith are already sages yet are still called "sentient beings" follows the designation of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The Tathāgata’s statement that they are "not sentient beings" follows the designation of the sages of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). That they are called "sentient beings" [in this context] refers to the sages.
"Non-dual" (*advaya*) is the name for the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Since it is called "non-dual," is it not indeed the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the very essence of Prajñā? △ Second, the direct manifestation [of the realization], in three parts: First, Subhūti presents his awakening.

2. First, equality of intrinsic nature; 3. Second, being fundamentally without deficiency or excess.
Subhūti, in my unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended;

This is intended to provide further confirmation. For what reason I have spoken thus and thus is that the Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment is the principle realized by the Buddha himself. If there were even a single dharma to be added, it could not be called "unsurpassed";

One must know that not only are there no manifold dharmas, but not even a single dharma can be apprehended. Even *anuttara-bodhi* itself has no dharma;

this explains that there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained. △ Second, the further explanation of equality.
By means of no-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas and thereby attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This serves as a further explanation for the reason why [the dharmas] are equal. It is precisely because those present and ready to receive the teaching might think that since principle is already equal, what need is there for cultivation, that the Buddha raised this point to provide a further explanation. There are simply two kinds of cultivation: first, cultivation according to characteristics; second, cultivation apart from characteristics. If one relies on cultivation according to characteristics...

What Subhūti has said below is that even wholesome dharmas are empty.

That which is called "wholesome dharmas" does not go beyond conforming to the Middle Way and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which shatters sentient beings' attachments to existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.

Viewed in this light, once the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) are discarded, the hundred negations are exhausted. Is this not the true mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the essence of the equality of self-nature? △
