To let the months and years slip by in vain, wasting away one's time, is the way of an ordinary person; for this reason, they are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).
You must know that when I usually speak of "ordinary beings," I am relying on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

When I speak of those who are "not ordinary beings," I am relying on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). And when I speak of them as being "merely named ordinary beings," I am relying on the Middle Way.
First, the Truth of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*). To clarify this: that which is "ordinary" is in fact non-ordinary;

it is only given the name "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*). This is called the emptiness of the ordinary person. Thus, above there is no Buddha who can deliver others, and below there are no ordinary persons to be delivered.
This is truly what is meant by "neither high nor low. Is this not precisely the equality of sentient beings and Buddhas? △ Second, Departing from [Duality].
3. Manifesting Equality through Emptiness and Existence.
First, abandoning the view of existence. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks?
Subhūti replied: "So it is, so it is. The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said: "Subhūti, if by..."
Regarding those who view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks: a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) would thus be the Tathāgata.
Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: “If one sees me by form, If one seeks me by sound, This is...”
"Those who walk in deviant paths cannot see the Tathāgata.
This passage dispels the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) to clarify that [the self] does not exist.

Indeed, the Buddha feared that people would fail to understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of non-self (*anātman*), and instead would grasp it as a substantial self (*ātman*). Therefore, he addressed the one present and asked: "Subhūti," [he said].
What do you think? Do ordinary people imagine that there is a "self" within me? Since they believe there is a self, they must necessarily have a body.
Having a physical form, they must necessarily possess the marks and signs; thus, they believe one can perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
The word "not" is used precisely to inquire whether this is possible or not. That is to say: is it possible, or is it not?
Yes. Previously it was said that one "sees" the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks; here it is said that one "contemplates" the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
To see with the eyes alone is called "seeing," while to employ both mind and eyes is called "contemplating. Although the eye and the mind differ, the apprehension of the marks is one and the same.
From the passage beginning with Subhūti, [the text] correctly clarifies that ordinary people, not knowing that the Buddha has no self yet speaking of a self, how could they...
One who is able to recognize the Buddha as being free from marks will naturally and inevitably perceive the Buddha by means of the thirty-two marks.
Therefore, the Buddha replied to him: "So it is, so it is. One perceives the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. This is a fixed principle.
From the words "The Buddha said, Subhūti" onwards, the Buddha explains that "Tathāgata" refers to the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. What...
This refers to the *dharmakāya* of true suchness (*tathatā*). Now, the *dharmakāya* is not a physical form;

how could it be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? If one were to insist on perceiving the Tathāgata solely through the thirty-two marks, then since a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) also possesses these thirty-two marks, he too would be the Tathāgata. Is such a principle possible? And...
The Wheel-Turning King is called a "Noble One" because he refrains from killing and guides people through the ten wholesome paths of action.
He also possesses the thirty-two marks; however, compared to those of a Buddha, they are slightly less distinct.
This is because the Buddha’s thirty-two marks manifest based upon the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), whereas the King’s thirty-two marks are based upon...
They arise from karmic causes. There are four types of such kings, namely those of gold, silver, copper, and iron. A golden-wheel king rules over the four continents;
a silver-wheel king, over three continents; a copper-wheel king, over two continents; and an iron-wheel king, over one continent.

Furthermore, when these holy kings are born, they are immediately endowed with the seven treasures. These are: first, the golden wheel treasure, named Supreme Sovereignty (*Vijaya-vaśavartin*); second...
1. The elephant treasure, named Green Mountain; 2. the horse treasure, named Swift Wind; 3.
the jewel treasure, named Cloud of Radiant Treasury; 4. the steward treasure, named Great Wealth; 5. the woman treasure, named Pure and Wondrous Virtue; 6.
the military commander treasure, named Stainless Eye. Possessing these seven treasures, he becomes a Wheel-Turning King. When he desires to go to the east, the wheel—
The precious wheel-cakra flies to the east; if it wishes to go west, the wheel-cakra proceeds to the west.

Should there be minor kingdoms that do not submit to its command, the wheel-cakra goes before them first, and they submit of their own accord without waiting for the use of weapons. Thus, he rules over the four continents and possesses a thousand sons.
His body is golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks, and is quite similar to that of a Buddha; he is the foremost being in the world.
He is a person of merit. From the passage where Subhūti addressed the Buddha downward, it is clearly seen that the Venerable One possesses a tongue without bone and eyes containing jewels;
he is accustomed to pushing a boat downstream with the current and also knows how to turn the rudder around a bend. Thus he said:
"As I understand the meaning of the Dharma-body being without marks as taught by the Buddha above, naturally one should not [use] the thirty..."
"Observing the Tathāgata through his two marks. The meaning intended by the one present at the occasion is that one observes the Buddha by means of his physical marks;
thus, the Wheel-Turning King is none other than the Tathāgata. If this were so, then one ought not to observe him by means of his marks.
Nevertheless, even though it is thus, it only expresses half of the truth. Why not bring forward these two lines before the Tathāgata had even spoken of the Wheel-Turning King? As it is said:
It follows the footsteps of others. Therefore, below this, the Tathāgata neither confirms it as correct nor rejects it as wrong;

he simply leaves it all aside without concern and speaks a verse. This is because the Buddha’s intention is that one should not perceive the Buddha by means of the thirty-two marks, nor say that the Tathāgata has any dharma to preach. Why?
Yes. This is because one fears that ordinary people who grasp at signs will give rise to false attachment. Therefore, it is said:
"Suppose all sentient beings were to take the form of the thirty-two marks as that which can see me, or take the sound of the Tathāgata’s fourfold eloquence and eightfold voice as such;
if they sought me by means of these," and so on, the text below concludes: "Such a person acts..."
This is the deviant path. Those who follow the deviant path fail to realize the equality of intrinsic nature; they rush outward in pursuit, seeking through words and grasping at signs.
How could this not be deviant? Therefore, it is said that they cannot see the Tathāgata. This means they themselves cannot see the Tathāgata, the Dharma-body free from signs.
This clarifies that signs are themselves signless, thereby eliminating the view of permanence and preventing people from becoming stagnant.
Regarding existence. △ Second, the elimination of the view of emptiness:
"Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of perfection, Subhūti, do not think thus;
it is not that the Tathāgata does not [attain it] by means of the marks of perfection."

Therefore, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, if you should think that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* preach the annihilation of all phenomena, do not hold such a thought.
Why is this? Those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
This demonstrates that [phenomena] are not empty by way of avoiding the view of nihilism; it is because, as stated in the preceding text, there is truly no dharma that arises as bodhicitta.
Focus the mind. Even for one who preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; in truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has brought to parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it is said that not even the slightest dharma exists by which one may attain bodhi. It is also said that one should not perceive the Buddha by means of the thirty-two marks.
Thus, all dharmas, including those concerning the causes and effects of the birth of a Buddha, are entirely empty. Yet, as for the Tathāgata...
This teaching is intended merely to demonstrate the equality of intrinsic nature by refuting the mind that clings to the existence of past phenomena.

However, I fear that those for whom this teaching is intended may fail to grasp its meaning; though they eliminate the grasping at existence, they may not avoid clinging to emptiness, mistakenly believing that this constitutes the realization of Bodhi.

There can certainly be no possession of the marks of perfection. If there were such possession of the marks, one would be a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) rather than one who has realized *bodhi*.
Why is this? Because one who has realized *bodhi* should not do so by virtue of possessing the marks.

If that were the case, one would have merely escaped the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*) only to fall into the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*). You must know that while the view of existence can be cured, the sickness of emptiness is difficult to treat.
What is called "vast emptiness" (hōtatsu kū) wherein there is no cause or effect—a state of vast, boundless indifference that invites calamity—is precisely what is meant by the saying:
"It is better to give rise to a view of existence as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of non-existence even as small as a mustard seed.
Once a person gives rise to such a view, they will forever become like withered wood or extinguished ashes, becoming a seed for the fetters of nihilism that entangle one in emptiness. Therefore, I...
The Tathāgata feared that although the disciple might understand that the marks of existence do not truly exist, he might nevertheless cling to a nihilistic emptiness.
For this reason, He called him by name and asked: "Subhūti, because you have heard such teachings as these above, do you think that all these dharmas are empty?
If you harbor such a thought, then consider this: when the Tathāgata attained Bodhi..."

"One should not [say] that it is by means of these marks of perfection. If one were to say so, it would be to deny the existence of the physical body and thereby fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, he calls out the name once more and warns him, saying: "Do not harbor such a thought. This is a most earnest and repeated exhortation;
one must absolutely not say that the Tathāgata attained *bodhi* without the marks of perfection. Why?
Thus, the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal. If one clings to its existence, it is the slander of superimposition;
if one clings to its non-existence, it is the slander of denial. It is not only that the existence of this Way is inadmissible; its non-existence is likewise inadmissible.
It is because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is without marks, yet there is nothing that is not without marks. Therefore, he calls out to him again, saying:

"O Subhūti, if you do not listen to my teaching, and instead continue to maintain the thought that one does not see the Buddha by means of specific marks, persisting in this without relinquishing it, and furthermore take such doctrines as 'in truth there are no dharmas' to be the ultimate limit—if this is so, then for all those who..."
Those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [claim] that there is neither cause nor effect, and thus teach that all phenomena (*dharma*) are subject to annihilation.

"All phenomena" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as the teachings on the causes and effects of the arising of supreme enlightenment and the Buddha.
To undermine the adornment of merit and virtue regarding the fruit, and to diminish the practice of the five perfections (*pāramitā*) regarding the cause—then...
One falls into the slander of nihilism and enters the pit of annihilation; the fault is exceedingly great. Therefore, I instruct you not to harbor such thoughts.

Why is this? It is said that one should not harbor such thoughts because, while it may be that one does not resolve [to attain enlightenment], those who are able to give rise to the bodhicitta will necessarily practice the six perfections and the four means of attraction, extensively performing Buddha-activities and benefiting others.
To benefit sentient beings, regarding the aforementioned dharmas, he certainly would not speak of the mark of annihilation.
This is because the emptiness of the Tathāgata is not the same as the emptiness of the non-Buddhists who eliminate obstructions to enter emptiness;

nor is it like the emptiness of the two vehicles, which merely cuts off views and afflictions, eliminates the分段 (fen-duan) birth-and-death, and realizes a partial emptiness. One must know that from the main teaching up to this point, all that has preceded—
Generally speaking, the Tathāgata speaks entirely of "wondrous existence" (miaoyou). This so-called wondrous existence is not existence;
therefore, he explains emptiness by means of existence itself. From this point onward, up until the section on "Circulation," all is the exposition of "true emptiness.

This so-called true emptiness is not empty; it is the elucidation of non-emptiness by means of emptiness itself. Thus we know that when existence does not abide in existence, only then is it called [true existence].

Wondrous existence. When emptiness does not stagnate in emptiness, it is first called "true emptiness. When the scriptural text reaches this point, having already transcended both emptiness and existence, and furthermore departed from both annihilationism and eternalism, is this not the meaning of the Middle Way, the true mark, and equanimity?

In this chapter, the Tathāgata calls out to the disciple three times, instructing him directly as if whispering into his ear; he does so precisely because he fears that the person may misinterpret the Buddha’s intent and recklessly discourse upon all phenomena.

All are empty. For this reason, I have admonished you again and again. Thus, the frequent calling of "Xiaoyu" was originally for no other purpose than to ensure that the husband could recognize the voice.
In short, if the eyes do not pursue forms, what harm is there in the green willows and red flowers?
If the ears do not follow sounds, one may let the orioles sing and the swallows chatter as they please. △ Third, comparing the superiority of merit in two parts: first, the comparison of superiority.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and give them as a gift, and if another person, knowing that all phenomena are without self, were to attain the patient acceptance [of non-arising], this bodhisattva would surpass the former bodhisattva regarding the merit obtained. Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.

This is because it was previously stated that one who penetrates the dharma of non-self is truly a bodhisattva, and it was further stated that when the Tathāgata speaks of a self, he does not mean there is a self.

However, as these doctrines of self and non-self may be difficult for people to clarify, the Buddha points to the present act of giving with signs to reveal the principle of the absence of dharmas. Thus, the Buddha addresses the one who is ready to receive the teaching.

It is said: "If there were a bodhisattva who, taking jewels from as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, used them for the purpose of giving, the merit thereof could indeed be called great.

This refers to matters involving signs (*sanimitta*). Furthermore, suppose there were another kind of person who, however, was unable to practice giving with jewels filling worlds as numerous as grains of sand, but who only knew the defilements of the mundane and supramundane realms..."

From the pure, the noble, and the ordinary, up to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve spheres (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)—all phenomena (*dharma*) are, in their very essence, entirely empty and devoid of self.
Upon realizing this emptiness, one does not dwell in emptiness; there is neither self nor the dharma of non-self.
Both [aspects] are accepted with patience (*kṣānti*). At its minimum, it lasts for the duration of a finger-snap; at its maximum, it endures for many years and months.
It is definitively confirmed and clearly understood, yet it is not expressed by the mouth, but is only endured within the mind.
Therefore, it is said that "patience is accomplished," which is precisely the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Yet, the subsequent comparison states: "this is the attainment of patience."
The Bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the Bodhisattva Jewel-Giver (*Ratnadatta*). This is because the one who gives jewels possesses a mind of grasping, and for that reason it is inferior;
whereas the one who has attained patience (*kṣānti*) possesses a non-conditioned mind, and for that reason it is superior. Why is this?
Below, the reason for this superiority is explained: the giving of jewels throughout sands of worlds does not equal [the merit of the latter].
Regarding those who have attained *kṣānti*: why is this so? Because these bodhisattvas, having already obtained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
They thoroughly understand that arising is non-arising; phenomena (*dharma*) are also non-phenomena. Arising is non-arising, yet this does not preclude non-arising from arising;
phenomena are also non-phenomena. What obstacle is there to non-phenomena being phenomena? If it is thus, who is it?
One receives merit. Who, then, does not receive merit? △ Second, the discussion on merit has two parts. First, the question on merit by the appropriate recipient:
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, why is it that a bodhisattva does not receive merit?"

At that time, because the interlocutor had heard [the teaching] that one does not receive merit, he had not yet grasped this principle; holding onto his doubts and unable to resolve them, he raised this question.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s answer regarding merit.
"Subhūti, the merit produced by a bodhisattva should not be grasped with attachment; therefore, it is said that 'merit is not received.
Because the Venerable One had not yet understood the meaning of 'not receiving merit,' the Buddha told him:
'Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to receive merit, that would be attachment to merit. This is why...'"
The teaching that a bodhisattva’s merit should not be clung to with greed—these two characters, "should not" (bù yīng), are words of admonition;
they mean that one must by no means cling to it. Why is this? For as soon as greed arises, it becomes outflowing (sāsrava).

If the cause is already with outflows (sāsrava), the fruit will also be with outflows; even if one possesses the thirty-two marks, such a person is merely equal to a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) and is not called a Buddha.
If one performs meritorious deeds alone without generating craving or attachment, then the cause becomes without outflows (anāsrava). Since the cause is already without outflows...
The fruit is likewise untainted (*anāsrava*). That which is obtained—the thirty-two marks that adorn the Dharma-body—is called "Buddha.
Because of this meaning of non-attachment, I say that a bodhisattva does not accept merit.

However, this "non-acceptance" does not mean rejecting the physical marks and signs born of a hundred merits, nor does it mean that the adornment of myriad virtues is not accepted; rather, it is as follows:
It is not because of greed or attachment that one does not receive; it is not a state of non-reception resulting from total absence.

What is meant is "non-greed and non-attachment," the "reception of non-reception," and "receiving while having no reception. One should understand that the preceding passage stated that the Tathāgata should not be viewed by means of the thirty-two marks;
this refers to the wondrous existence that is not existent, which is free from the view of permanence. Now, do not act in this way.
Contemplate this: The Tathāgata does not attain Bodhi by means of the marks of perfection. This is the emptiness that is not empty; it is free from the view of nihilism.
To observe the Buddha preaching the Dharma is truly like a gourd on the water: press down and it immediately turns over, like a jewel in the sunlight.
Form has no fixed shape. If one says that the Tathāgata is without marks, one does not know that the Tathāgata is precisely the marks.
If one says that the Tathāgata is both the marks and without marks, one does not know that the Tathāgata is neither the marks nor without marks.

If one claims that what is not the characteristic is itself the characteristic, one falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). If one claims that the characteristic is itself the absence of characteristic, one further establishes the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

One must know that by being neither identical nor both, only then can the views of eternalism and nihilism be extinguished. Having thus departed from the views of eternalism and nihilism, [one attains liberation].
Thus, it cannot be constrained by emptiness; how could this not be the meaning of the equality of True Suchness? △ Third, revealing equality through the absence of coming and going:
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person...
Understand the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this? One who comes from nowhere and goes nowhere is therefore called a Tathāgata.
This clarifies that the Dharma-body has no coming or going, manifesting the principle of equality. Now, because of the preceding passage: "If by..."
To seek the Buddha through forms or to pursue him through sounds is to be unable to see the Buddha's verse. One might fear that someone would say:

"The Tathāgata is currently present within the four modes of deportment—speaking and remaining silent, moving and staying still—and all who have eyes behold him and all who have ears hear him; how can you say he is not seen?"
Therefore, the Buddha called out to those present and addressed them, saying: "Suppose there were someone who spoke thus,
thinking that they had seen me— whether I entered Śrāvastī, or returned to Jetavana, or sat cross-legged at times,
or lay down in the auspicious posture at times— if such were the case, this person would not understand what I have said above."
This is indeed so. Why? For I have previously stated that "Tathāgata" means the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Since it is the meaning of suchness, how could there be any characteristics of coming or going, or any reality of sitting or reclining?
This is merely to manifest the human dharma and respond to worldly affairs. If one were to seek it within the body of the Dharma-body itself, even its form and appearance cannot be found.
It is said that the path of language is severed and the tracks of mental activity are cut off; how, then, could such a thing exist?

Therefore, the subsequent text provides an inquiry and explanation, saying: "That which cannot be seen through speech or silence, motion or stillness, coming or going, sitting or lying down—why is this so?
It is because the Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas; his essence is the true mark (dharmatā), which is non-existent [in terms of conceptual constructs]."

There is no appearance that is not non-appearance. Even if there were coming and going or sitting and reclining, these would all be nothing other than manifestations shown in response to sentient beings.
Not only did he come from the Jeta Grove in the present; though it is said he came, there was no coming. Even if he had come from Tuṣita, he would likewise have never come.
Not only did he depart from Śrāvastī; though it is said he departed, there was no departing. Even if he later went toward the Twin Trees, he likewise would have never gone.
He has indeed departed. Judging by this principle, for the Tathāgata, coming with the characteristic of non-coming is true coming;
for sentient beings, seeing with the characteristic of non-seeing is deluded seeing. One must know that if the Tathāgata has already come, he does not come again;
if he has already departed, he does not depart again. This is what is meant by "coming from nowhere" and "departing to nowhere."
Wherever one arrives, that which was previously visible can no longer be seen. Therefore, it is said that there is nowhere from which one comes, nor anywhere to which one goes.
Because there is thus neither coming nor going, one is called the Tathāgata.

Even when the Tathāgata engages in the ordinary activities of daily life—coming and going, sitting and reclining—it is no more than clouds moving and the moon shifting, or a boat traveling while the shore appears to move.
It moves; yet the moon has never traveled, nor has the shore ever shifted—it is merely a matter of following one's own perceptions.
It is also like the moon’s reflection in water: one does not know that the moon is not printing upon the water, yet the water prints itself.
This precisely concludes the preceding case concerning the journey from Śrāvastī to Jetavana, up until the passage where he spreads his seat and sits; it is simply "no coming."
[The Buddha] then sat down and lay down to demonstrate the meaning of equality. 4. Revealing Equality through the Non-One and the Many:
"Subhūti, suppose a good man or a good woman were to grind this trichiliocosm into fine dust.
What do you think? Would that mass of dust be great? "It would be very great, World-Honored One. "Why is that?"
If these multitudes of atoms were real entities, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as "multitudes of atoms. Why is this?
That which the Buddha calls a "multitude of atoms" is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely designated as a "multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata speaks of as a "trichiliocosm" is not a world; it is merely designated as a "world. For what reason? If the world...
That which is a truly existent realm is a unified whole (*piṇḍa-grāha*). The Tathāgata says that a unified whole is not a unified whole;
it is merely called a "unified whole. Subhūti, a unified whole is inexpressible;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.
Having clarified above that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya neither comes nor goes, there may be those who say:

"That which comes and goes is the Nirmāṇakāya; that which neither comes nor goes is the Dharmakāya. When it resides among sentient beings, it has coming and going; when it resides in the Buddha, it has no coming or going.
If this were so, the three bodies would be distinct from one another, and the sentient being and the Buddha would be at odds. How could this be called "equanimity" (píng)?
This is the meaning of "equality. Therefore, the Buddha uses the three types of worlds currently known to all people as an analogy to clarify this point.
Thus, within this context, it is only when one provides a threefold interpretive explanation that the principle will be fully elucidated.

These are: first, the container world (*bhājana-loka*); second, the sentient world (*sattva-loka*); and third, the world of ultimate direct realization. Now, first following the text regarding the container world:
Aggregation and dispersal clarify that things are neither one nor many, and that they are without going or coming.

In this context, it is said that Subhūti, if there should be virtuous sons or daughters of good family in the world who are able to cultivate the contemplation of analyzing form until it returns to emptiness:

Furthermore, suppose one were to divide a great trichiliocosm into seven parts each, and then divide those parts again and again until they were reduced to the most minute atoms (*paramāṇu*). What do you think?
If one were to calculate the number of such extremely subtle atoms produced by dividing such a vast world into pieces?
"O Assembly, do you think that this is much or not? This was intended to examine whether it was indeed much or not. The meaning behind the words of the assembly was:
"If even a world-system of such vast proportions were ground into dust, it would be difficult for the divine eye of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to fully comprehend it;
how then could it be measured by numbers? Therefore, they said, "It is very much. World-Honored One, yet this "very much" is...

The Venerable One answered according to the questions posed. What follows is a critical examination and explanation; this is precisely the Venerable One taking a different path. His intention is as follows:
"My many answers were nothing other than discussing matters based on specific matters; because the questions were many, the answers were many.
Nevertheless, although the most minute particles (*paramāṇu*) may appear numerous, they possess no substantial reality and thus cannot be said to be 'many'."
Why is this so? If these numerous subtle particles possessed a real, substantial essence, the Buddha would not have called them "a multitude of subtle particles.
This clarifies their lack of substantiality and correctly reveals that the nature of the particles is empty.
Furthermore, below, he uses the essence and form to clarify the contemplation of emptiness, thereby demonstrating that the subtle particle is neither form nor emptiness.

This is precisely because [all things] are subsumed within the three truths. Therefore, when I say that "the number of atoms is exceedingly great," it is merely spoken in accordance with worldly convention.
If one were to discuss this from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), not even a single atom could be established, for the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
How much more so, then, would atoms themselves not be empty? It is said that where a single atom is empty, there all atoms are likewise empty.
Emptiness. Within the emptiness of the multitude of atoms, a single atom is empty; within the emptiness of a single atom, there is no multitude of atoms;
within the emptiness of the multitude of atoms, there is no single atom. Discussed from this perspective, it is said that they are "not indeed a multitude of atoms.
If one discusses them according to the ultimate truth of the Middle Way, then the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only; what need is there to speak of atoms?

They are not atoms; originally they are a single substance, identical in being True Suchness (tathatā). What obstacle could there be to provisional names? Thus it is said: "This is called a multitude of subtle atoms.
At this point, the world is entirely dispersed into subtle atoms; in the following passage, the subtle atoms are then gathered back together to form the world.
The intention of the interlocutor is that not only are the atoms thus, but so too is the world itself.

It is likewise so. Therefore, it is called "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*). As previously stated, that great trichiliocosm which can be crushed into atoms is merely formed by the aggregation of atoms; how could it possess any substantial reality?
Therefore, it is said to be "not a world. This precisely clarifies that the nature of the realm is empty. Nevertheless, it is a realm of the mind-only. Thus...
Nor does it abolish conventional designations; therefore, it is said, "This is called a world. Furthermore, to investigate and explain this:

if it is said that "it is not," yet also stated that "this is called [a world]," for what reason? Following the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one speaks of the "trichiliocosm" (*mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*);
following the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one says "it is not a world"; and following the middle way, the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one transcends both affirmation and negation.
It is neither "is" nor "is not. That which is neither "is" nor "is not" is called a "world. Looking downward, it connects with the preceding fine dust;
looking forward, it penetrates to the subsequent world. To summarize and inquire into all of this at once: if both the dust and the world are empty, for what reason is this so?
If the fine dust and the world were truly possessed of a substantial essence, they would constitute a "unified whole" (*ekaghanākāra*). This is what is meant by a "unified whole."
This refers to being one by virtue of being neither two nor distinct; to be joined means not to be separated or dispersed. Now, however, it is not so.
Since the world can be broken down into subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), every atom is then separated and dispersed;
it is not the case that they are not separated or dispersed. Since subtle atoms can be joined together to form a world, every part of the world is then dual and...
It is not that there is neither duality nor difference. Viewed from this perspective, both the sense objects and the realms lack intrinsic nature;
they are empty in their very essence, and even the characteristic of their "unified totality" cannot be apprehended. Therefore, it is said:
"The Tathāgata speaks of a unified totality, yet it is not a unified totality. The reason he speaks of a unified totality is that he does so in accordance with worldly convention.
To speak of them as neither one nor a composite accords with reality. To speak of them as being "named" is for the sake of conforming to the Middle Way.
Indeed, when the world-system is first broken down into atoms, one perceives only the multiplicity of atoms and does not perceive the oneness of the world-system;

yet now, at the point where those atoms are recombined into a world-system, one perceives only the oneness of the world-system and does not perceive the multiplicity of atoms. One must understand that this process of breaking down the world-system [is the very basis of our understanding].
It is reduced to atoms. This is "many" yet not many, clarifying that the many come from nowhere and go nowhere.
When atoms combine to form the world, this is "one" yet not one, clarifying that the one comes from nowhere and the many go nowhere.
Therefore, although it is many, it is not many; it does not preclude speaking of "many" in accordance with the atoms. Although it is one, it is not one.
What prevents us from speaking of "one" in relation to the world? This refers to the atoms of the world; they are neither one nor many, yet they are both many and one without contradiction.
This concludes the explanation regarding the *bhājana-loka* (the physical environment).

Next, secondly, the explanation will proceed in relation to the *sattva-loka* (sentient beings), interpreting it through the lens of true and false form and mind. For the *sattva-loka* consists of both the true and the false.
"Matter and mind" refers to the great trichiliocosm, which is an analogy for the minds of sentient beings.

"Shattering them into dust" precisely represents the arising of delusion from the truth, whereby the deluded mind becomes consciousness; thus, the various waves of consciousness surge and arise in succession.
From the single dharma of the One Mind, the aspects of subject and object (xiàngjiàn) arise; because of these aspects of subject and object, the five aggregates and the six sense bases arise.

The twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and even the six million six hundred eighty-four thousand dharmas—when it is said that these are "extremely numerous," it is precisely a metaphor for the sands of ignorance (*avidyā*).

When it is said that the nature of minute particles is empty, this serves as an analogy for the emptiness of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the emptiness of the nature of sentient beings (*sattva*). In terms of the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), minute particles are neither one nor many.

The primary analogy is that True Suchness (tathatā) is neither one nor different. All that precedes this concerns the arising of delusion from the True, wherein the deluded mind becomes consciousness;
this serves as an analogy for sentient beings' "going" [to rebirth]. Although they go, they have not truly gone, and thus it is said that there is nowhere to which they go.
What follows concerns the formation of the realms by clinging to sensory objects; this correctly parallels sentient beings returning from delusion to the True. As for the "great trichiliocosm":
This is the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*). That which is "not a world" is the very essence of True Suchness;

it is the fulfillment of Bodhi, returning to the state of non-attainment. This is what is called a "world. By analogy, True Suchness pervades all places and possesses the function of responding to conditions (*pratyaya*).
Thus, the subtle dusts mentioned above are neither many nor not many; they are precisely within the mind of True Suchness.

Originally, there were no names or characteristics for the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of form and mind; yet, they have come to be established as the names and characteristics of the five aggregates of form and mind.
Within this, multiplicity is non-dual unity; it is precisely *tathatā* (suchness) that is identical with the dharmas of the five aggregates of form and mind.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "In this way, even the five aggregates, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen..."
The "Dhātu" (Realm), the "Original Tathāgatagarbha," and the "Sublime Nature of True Suchness" refer to this very point.
Although sentient beings awaken to this True Suchness and are thus called "Tathāgatas" (Thus-Come Ones), they have not actually come; therefore, it is said that they "come from nowhere.

Third, regarding the world of ultimate true awakening, if explained through the categories of Dharma-body, Response-body, and Transformation-body, then the great trichiliocosm is the quiescent light of the Dharmakāya.
As for "the realm being broken into subtle particles," this means that from the essence arises function, and from the Truth arises transformation.

As for "being exceedingly numerous," this refers to the manifestation of bodies according to the various classes of beings, such that there is nowhere they do not exist. As for "the empty nature of the subtle particles," this serves as an analogy for how the manifested response is not the ultimate reality.
Speaking in terms of the Three Truths, the subtle particles are neither empty nor existent; this is used as an analogy for the [manifested] response.
These transformations all arise from the Dharma-body; they are neither real nor unreal. This clarifies that function arises from essence, and transformation arises from the truth.
They emerge from within the suchness of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). One must know that although they come, there is no coming;

thus, their coming has no point of origin. Hence it is said that "they come from nowhere. Yet, when they unite with sensory objects to form realms, this illustrates the subsuming of function back into essence.

This refers to gathering and transforming beings so they return to the truth. "The great trichiliocosm" is the one true dharma-realm, the land of eternal quiescent light, the true sphere of the Dharma-body.
"That which is not a world" means that the Dharma-body is free from all marks.
"That which is called a world" illustrates how the Dharma-body pervades all places; there is nowhere among all sentient beings or lands where it does not go.
Yet it is not the Dharma-body. Discussing this in terms of the Three Truths, the world is neither existent nor empty;
by analogy, the Dharma-body is both identical with and distinct from its marks, neither one nor different. This, then, subsumes the response and transformation bodies within True Suchness.
It departs; yet it departs without departing, for there is nowhere to which it departs. Thus it is said: "There is also no place to which it goes."
Thus concludes the explanation of the three kinds of worlds according to their respective categories. Below, these three are synthesized to clarify the "unified totality" (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*).
This unified totality, if situated within the world of the vessel (*bhājanaloka*), is called the true realm of *śāntaprabhāsvara* (tranquil light).

If situated within the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), it is termed the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness), the fundamental essence of Buddha-nature. If situated within the world of true awakening (*dharmaloka*), it is termed *viśuddha* (purity).

The pure Dharma-body is what is called neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different. For this reason, when the Tathāgata speaks of a "unified mass," it is precisely because it is not a unified mass;
these are exactly such designations. Although it belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is established in contrast to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If one were in the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single atom could be established; how then could there be such things?

This is the designation for it. To call this "the mark of a single integration" precisely clarifies that the three worlds—the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, as well as the animate and the inanimate—all possess this principle. Therefore, the Tathāgata’s seal states:
"The mark of a single integration is that which cannot be spoken. This refers precisely to the fact that this principle is neither identical nor different, neither real nor empty. What is...
This refers to opening one's mouth to form a pair of stakes, or raising one's eyebrows to let two or three things fall. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma cannot be shown;

words and signs are quiescent. This is precisely what that means. As for why I now speak of the "unified mark" (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*), it is nothing more than because worldly ordinary people are greedily attached to such things that I speak of the unified mark. This is exactly as the Tathāgata [taught].
The matters of a lifetime’s heart, which have never been disclosed to others, are all spoken within the state of non-speaking.
One must know that throughout the forty-nine years, [the Buddha] did nothing other than address those ordinary people who grasp at signs and cling to phenomena;
therefore, he did not speak three times for three reasons, nor did he speak once for one reason. Ultimately, within the Tathāgata’s original ground, there was originally nothing at all.
The identity of the three is thus attainable. △ Fifth, revealing equality by means of various views:
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span," what do you think, Subhūti?
Would that person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One. That person would not."

One understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this? The World-Honored One speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span;

yet these are not actually the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span. They are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."

This serves as a general refutation of all attachments in order to reveal the correct wisdom of the three kinds of emptiness. This is because it was stated in the "Chapter on Detachment from Marks" at the beginning of the sutra:
"If a bodhisattva were to claim that there are beings to be saved, they would then be attached to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Non-Abiding," it says: "If the mind grasps at marks, one is attached to the four marks; if one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one is attached to the four [marks]."

Regarding characteristics: if one grasps at the characteristic of non-dharma, one is immediately attached to the four characteristics. Viewed in this light, these four characteristics are the very means by which the sutra can sweep away all attachments.
Therefore, when the Buddha reached this point, he questioned the one present who was ready to receive the teaching, saying:
"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to say that as soon as the Tathāgata opens his mouth, he speaks of the four characteristics—what would you say?"
"Can this person still understand the meaning of what I, the Tathāgata, have spoken? Is it that he understands, or does he not?
When the disciple reached this point, he profoundly realized the essence of equality and skillfully comprehended the Buddha’s mind; therefore, he replied:
"No. How could worldly people understand this meaning? They assume that because the Tathāgata speaks of the four characteristics everywhere, there must truly be four characteristics to be found.
Furthermore, how could they understand that these four characteristics are neither existent nor empty?
Therefore, [the text] uses the question "Why is this so? to provide the explanation: "Because the World-Honored One has taught that our four..."
To speak of "seeing" accords with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). To say that there is no "self" and so forth among the four views accords with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
To say that these are called the four views of "self" and so forth accords with the Middle Way, the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If this is so, then...
Thus, when the Buddha spoke of our four views, the meaning encompasses the Three Truths.

He intended for all sentient beings to realize that "I" is precisely "not-I," and that "no-self" is "self," thereby clearly understanding their own nature and suddenly realizing the wondrous existence of true emptiness.
How could those ordinary people and followers of external paths ever comprehend this? If one relies on the removal of attachments to reveal emptiness...
Regarding the commentary: when the Buddha speaks of "our four views," this refers to ordinary people and non-Buddhists who grasp at signs according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

it is intended to eliminate the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). When he says they are "not four views," this refers to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who grasp at the characteristics of phenomena according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
it is intended to eliminate the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). When he says "these are called the four views," this refers to the middle [truth].
When a Bodhisattva on the stage of the Path takes up the mark of non-dharmas (*adharmalakṣaṇa*), it is to eliminate attachment to non-dharmas.
Thus, all three attachments are simultaneously dispelled. [It is] neither real nor unreal; neither empty nor existent. This is the meaning of the equality of the Middle Way.
Regarding the first chapter of the five chapters which clarifies "sentient beings and Buddhas," this refers to the holy and the ordinary.

Second, regarding the views of emptiness and existence, they do not belong to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism. Third, because there is no coming or going, both the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the transformation-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) are equally eliminated.
The above clarifies that the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*) cannot be apprehended, thereby demonstrating equality.

Fourth, by means of the one and the many, it is shown that the nature of the objective realm is empty; since the unity is not a unified whole, the secondary retribution (*upādāyabhoga*) cannot be apprehended. This is because...
Although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they do not transcend the dharmas of the sacred and the ordinary, the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, and so forth.
Each of these has been elucidated to lead directly back to the equal fundamental essence. Now, the dharmas grasped through attachment are all simultaneously dispensed with and swept away;
hence there is this Fifth Chapter. Indeed, since the Tathāgata first opened this assembly, he has consistently employed these four views to eliminate [delusion].
People cling to their own sentiments; [this teaching] unfolds the principle of equality.

Now that the essence of equality has been revealed and its meaning further clarified, both [the previous teachings and these attachments] are swept away together. As it is said, "When the illness is cured, there is no need for the physician.
Thus, the Buddha’s previous teaching of the raft parable—that even the Dharma should be relinquished—is indeed true. △ Third, the conclusion of the beginning.
The Final Chapter on Dharmas.

Subhūti, one who has set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all dharmas, know them thus, see them thus, and resolve with faith thus, so that no conception of dharmas arises. Subhūti, as for what is called "dharmas"—
Regarding "characteristics": the Tathāgata says that what is called a characteristic of dharmas is, in fact, not a characteristic of dharmas;

this is what is meant by the "characteristic of dharmas. This statement summarizes and concludes the meaning of the entire sutra. For at the beginning of the sutra, the appropriate recipient had asked:
"How should a good man or a good woman who has resolved their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
"One should abide [in this state]. How does one subdue the mind? The World-Honored One has already elucidated this in general;
here, he concludes by saying: "If there are sons or daughters of good family who have truly resolved upon Bodhicitta, they should know thus, see thus, and believe and understand thus.
These three phrases correctly conclude the question-and-answer section of this sutra. As for... [the following is as in the original].
Previously, when you asked me how one should abide, I instructed you to abide with a mind that has no abiding, not dwelling upon objects such as the six sense-fields;
you should understand it in this way. Previously, when you asked me how one should subdue [the mind], I instructed you to deliver all sentient beings;
having delivered all sentient beings, one does not perceive any sentient being to be delivered.

“Dharmodgata, you should view it in this way. Regarding your previous question to me concerning the method for generating the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I have taught you that generating the mind through the non-existence of phenomena (*dharma*) is the true generation of the mind.
You should believe and understand it in this way. If one can know it thus, that is true knowledge; if one sees it thus, that is true vision.”

To have faith and understanding in this way is true faith and understanding. Nevertheless, even so, one must not give rise to the conceptualization of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) before one can succeed.

Why is this? If one were to cling to the teaching that there is definitively no abiding and that one is free from characteristics—that there are no dharmas—this would again be to take the medicine and turn it into a disease.
Therefore, the reason the Tathāgata teaches the characteristics of dharmas is to accord with the principle of truth (*satyadharma*).

Thus it is said. Therefore, to accord with worldly convention is to speak of "dharmalakṣaṇa" (phenomenal characteristics); to accord with the truth is to say "not dharmas"; and to accord with the Middle Way is to say "this is merely a name.
This is the fundamental purport of our Tathāgata’s discourse on the single realm of Prajñāpāramitā and the three truths:
neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor distinct, neither existent nor empty. Therefore, he speaks of "this is merely a name" as the phenomenal characteristic.
Listen! What is meant is the wondrous existence of true emptiness, which is neither existent nor empty.

If this is so, then flowers, incense, documents, and powders all return to the definitive and true expression; the forms of water and the countenances of mountains are entirely in accord with the wondrous truth of suchness (*tathatā*).
Inferring from this, every atom, every world-system, every phenomenon, and every particular—none are not the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. This clarifies...
The Main Body of the Teaching concludes.
△ Third, the Dissemination [of the Teaching], in two parts. First, showing the exhortation for dissemination. Second, showing the benefits of disseminating the sutra.
Subhūti, if there were someone who took the seven treasures of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and used them as an offering in almsgiving.
If there are good sons or good daughters who have resolved their minds on Bodhi and uphold this sutra— even as little as a single four-line verse—
receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others, their merit shall surpass that of the former.

This clarifies that the benefit of this sutra surpasses even the most precious jewels. Within the text, it speaks of "arousing bodhicitta," for by upholding it oneself and teaching it to others, one eternally ensures the lineage of the Buddhas.
It is taught for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, and it is taught for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).
Were it not for those who have aroused the mind of the Supreme Vehicle, they would be unable to uphold or expound this sutra; this is because its merit is superior.

"That person" refers precisely to one who is able to uphold this sutra; that such a person surpasses the gift of immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) treasures to the Sangha demonstrates the benefit of mastering the sutra.
△ Second, showing the method for mastering the sutra.
How should one expound the Dharma for others? Without grasping at marks, remaining as suchness, unmoving. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way.

This clarifies the method for interpreting the sutras. It was precisely because my Tathāgata, out of a compassionate heart, considered the future and wished to bestow grace upon those to come, that he specifically singled this out and spoke of it at the conclusion of the Dharma assembly.
"Not grasping at marks" means not grasping at the four marks, such as self, phenomena, non-phenomena, and so forth; and it also refers to not grasping at words.
This explains that the mind takes the characteristics of names as its objects. Regarding the phrase "as-it-is and immovable": "as-it-is" (ruru) means being as it is within True Suchness (tathatā).
"Immovable" refers to the very essence of True Suchness. This is the correct teaching for those who propagate the sutras:
they awaken to the principle of as-it-is, give rise to the wisdom of as-it-is, and expound the Dharma of as-it-is, thereby benefiting themselves and others alike.
This is the realization of the essence of the immovable vajra. One must know that to grasp at signs is to move; to move is to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Not to grasp is to be unmoving;
to be unmoving is to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, to grasp at signs is not to accord with suchness (*tathatā*), whereas suchness does not grasp at signs.
This intent precisely elucidates the three kinds of *prajñā*, concluding by returning to the title of the treatise.

This is the essential meaning. "Expounding it for others" refers to the *prajñā* of words and letters (*vyañjana-prajñā*). "Not grasping at appearances" refers to the *prajñā* of contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*).
"Unmoving in suchness" refers to the *prajñā* of the true reality (*dharmatā-prajñā*). This is precisely how the Tathāgata instructs sentient beings of the末法 (final dharma) age:
those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta and expound [the Dharma] for others must not grasp at appearances, but must abide securely [in the truth].
Within the equality of True Suchness (tathatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one must first attain certainty and freedom from doubt;

only then can one raise the whisk and lift the eyebrows, all of which are the primary meaning (paramārtha). As for "expounding," it means to give rise to contemplative observation (vipaśyanā) through words and letters, and to awaken to the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) by means of that observation.
If this is so, then this is truly to shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is *samyaksambodhi*. Therefore, the inquiry and explanation state: one must certainly not grasp at signs. Why is this?

Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world—namely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*)—are merely that which sentient beings within the three realms of existence falsely cling to as existing; they are nothing more than such [illusory appearances].
They are merely like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dewdrops, and lightning; fundamentally, they lack reality.
How could they be grasped as the marks of a self, a person, and so forth? Therefore, it is said that one should contemplate them in this way. Question:
Since these marks are all unreal, being entirely like dharmas such as dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, where then is the *tathatā* (suchness)?
[The Master] moved. [The Disciple] replied: "It is not that the teaching intends to cast away all dharmas;

rather, if one does not give rise to attachments to the marks of self, person, and so forth regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), then those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) are themselves the true mind of Prajñā, the very essence of Suchness (*tathatā*).
As the ancients said: "Simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness. This is precisely it. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*...
Yan said: "The five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
He further said: "If you simply do not follow after the discrimination of worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings, then because these three conditions are severed..."
When the three causes do not give rise [to delusion], then the madness of your own mind—your *Yajñadatta*—will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself *bodhi*.
This intrinsically pure and luminous mind has always been coextensive with the *dharmadhātu*; it is not obtained from others. Why rely on arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?
Why grasp at various appearances? Once you can ensure that the mind does not grasp at appearances, then every phenomenon is *tathatā* (suchness). Since...
All phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*). How could one negate the myriad existences before they can be called unmoving suchness? This is precisely what Master Pang said:
"If you yourself are without mind toward the myriad things, what prevents the myriad things from constantly surrounding you? Indeed, it is thus.
Only then can one respond to conditions through transformation, enter the marketplace with hands extended, and—dragging through mud and water—benefit humans and devas.
△ Second, the formal conclusion on the circulation [of this teaching].
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world— including gods, humans, and asuras— having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.

"Believing, accepting, and practicing"—this refers to the correct acceptance and circulation [of the teaching]. "The Elder," and so forth, refers to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.
Regarding the phrase "joyfully practicing," according to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, there are three meanings: first, the purity of the speaker.
It is not for the sake of gain or sustenance; second, it is pure in what is taught, knowing the Dharma as it truly is; third, it is pure in the attainment of the fruit.
Therefore, one should joyfully practice it. One should know that these are the words of Ānanda during the compilation [of the Canon], meaning:
Whenever one hears the Dharma with joy, there will inevitably be a wondrous resonance within the mind. Thus, through resonance comes faith; through faith comes acceptance;
and once accepted, it must be put into practice. At that time, after Puwen had composed this commentary, he joined his palms in homage to the Buddha and spoke these words:

I prostrate to the Vajra Supreme Being, To the inconceivable and profound Prajñā, And to all the sages and worthies gathered throughout the Jeta Grove. May you grant your compassion and bestow your protection upon me;
Now, like measuring the great ocean with a conch-shell, I vainly attempt to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom with an ordinary mind.
May I immediately realize the four views in accord with suchness, And swiftly attain the path of the equality of Bodhi.
For the sake of benefiting future beings submerged in darkness, Not for my own sake nor seeking fame and honor,
I universally pray that all sentient beings throughout the realms, Upon seeing, hearing, or rejoicing in this, may all attain Buddhahood.
Commentary on the Heart Seal of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Lower (End)
